prs.title: fix: allow larger managed repository ref inventories
prs.body: Fixes #177856. ## What Problem This Solves Starting a worktree from a branch that exists upstream but is missing from a managed clone can fail before workspace preparation when the repository has many remote refs. Both the inventory before fetching and the inventory afterward inherit a 256 KiB command-output cap. The complete list can exceed that cap even though every ref is valid, so retrying the session repeats the same failure. ## User Impact Managed-repository sessions can refresh larger complete inventories and create their worktree at the requested commit. An inventory that exceeds the supported bound still stops safely, with an error that identifies the limit and suggests an already-available base or administrator assistance. The message no longer assumes that the repository contains obsolete branches. Default-branch creation, branch suggestions, checkout ownership, cancellation and the recorded remote identity retain their existing behavior. This change adds no configuration, schema, dependency or protocol requirement. ## Why This Change Was Made The ref reader now uses its own 8 MiB stdout allowance while keeping diagnostic stderr at 256 KiB. Both inventory reads share this owner. Successful exit, untruncated output and valid records remain required before an inventory can drive tracking-ref updates or pruning. The regression coverage exercises complete large inventories on both sides of the fetch, preserves the record-aligned truncation case at the new limit, and verifies that failed inventories leave the existing packed refs unchanged. The existing session retry test now uses a large managed clone and checks the requested branch's distinct commit and file contents. The worktree documentation explains the limit and recovery guidance. ## Evidence The prior controlled reproduction used 7,852 refs / 808,708 bytes. The original code failed both the initial-inventory and fetched-inventory scenarios; retries failed without creating a worktree or changing the canonical refs. Small-repository, default-base and already-present-base controls passed. An isolated candidate with the same inventory allowance passed those startup scenarios and the surrounding Git/worktree coverage. Separate real-Git probes refreshed 50,000 refs / 6.4 MB and rejected overflow both before and after fetch with canonical refs unchanged. These are Linux synthetic-repository results, not a claim of production deployment or unlimited repository size. Remote formatting, scoped lint and all selected production/test compiler graphs passed. Auto Review reported no actionable P0–P2 findings in the supplied source. The two changed test files passed all 37 tests via `pnpm test src/projects/project-registry.test.ts src/gateway/server-methods/sessions-create-worktree-base.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 74.44 seconds for the session-handler file and 21.95 seconds for the registry file, with 124.25 seconds total including worker preparation. The large-inventory success cases took 1.49 seconds each; overflow rejection took 0.22 seconds before fetch and 4.78 seconds afterward. Seven related test files passed another 100 tests in 142.46 seconds, covering clone registration, authority, repository materialization and Git fetch/session creation. Independent engineering review is clean. Hosted CI passed all 53 selected jobs; 27 jobs were intentionally unselected. The two changed files also passed all 37 cases in CI: 8.638 seconds of registry case time and 22.596 seconds of session-handler case time. These are summed case durations, not whole-job or billing measurements. A real-Gateway Chromium run has now verified the failed-start/retry sequence on this exact source: 7,852 refs / 832,258 bytes, one session creation, one retry through the existing composer, the same session key and route, and a real worktree at the newly published branch's distinct commit with its expected file. All prior refs remained, and the synthetic model reply appeared. Git inventory/refresh, Gateway RPC, persistence, checkout and browser behavior were real; the Git source transport and model endpoint used isolated synthetic fixtures. The identical sequence on the unfixed base reproduced the inventory error on both attempts and created no worktree. Both builds served identical UI bytes at 1440 × 1000; screenshots and the fixed-head recording below show the result. The requested commit in the successful run was `d94710667eecb770855a255aac01c15c34508c03`, verified with Git along with the expected file contents. Only the private worker name is masked in the recording; its initial one-second loading lead-in is removed. ## Visual evidence []() | Before | After | | --- | --- | | ![Unfixed Gateway rejects the large inventory again after the branch is published; no worktree is created\.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/40683448-23c2-4ede-8257-29ef3e0d8570) | ![Fixed Gateway recovers in the same session and shows the assistant reply after creating the requested worktree\.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4aa5f6ca-b871-408c-9820-5a426b44eebd) | ### Exact\-head creation, initial missing\-branch error, and successful same\-session retry https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/195b9a72-0748-4adc-a865-803fe6381f34 ### Visual verification - Baseline: 0449ef26b26630eba2c75cb53262bee23343e31c - Exact head: `11c774f42bc42140b63ae28c3f7c1fb1b3bc2976` - Scenario: Start a worktree at origin/new\-branch in a managed clone with 7,852 refs\. Publish the previously absent branch upstream, then retry through the same chat composer\. - Runtime/build: OpenClaw Gateway CLI \(dist/index\.js\) built from PR source tree a0d27daeae0859392216f64429ec466112f078c0, Linux Chromium\. Served UI SHA\-256: 6cd5f11418866100b060315edc8e8c2ef16f4e072996c65574d3abf22cdbf812\. - Inventory: Initial clone in both builds: 7,852 refs / 832,258 bytes - Before: Initial preparation and retry both reject the inventory; zero worktrees; original refs unchanged - After: Retry creates the worktree at requested commit d94710667eecb770855a255aac01c15c34508c03 and verifies new\-branch\.txt contents - Session continuity: One sessions\.create, one chat\.send, same session key and route - Ref preservation: Every prior ref remains after successful refresh - Fixture boundaries: Real Gateway, Git, persistence, worktree and browser\. Synthetic local Git transport and loopback model endpoint\. - Matched viewport, theme, repository structure, ref count, input sequence and served UI bytes - Gateway run and browser scenario passed on both baseline and exact candidate - Screenshots inspected at native resolution; full recording timeline inspected from sequential decoded frames - Only private worker\-name text masked; initial one\-second loading lead\-in removed; triggering actions and results preserved - No live Team deployment or external GitHub/model\-provider claim

prs.title: fix: streamed replies with a leaked model control token no longer re-scan the whole reply
prs.body:
Fixes #175444

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a streamed reply that contains one leaked model control token (for example `<|assistant|>`) re-scans the entire reply on every later delta, costing seconds of Gateway event-loop CPU per reply and growing quadratically — 5.6 s at 65 KB and 23.4 s at 128 KB on `main` at 51ebf30c8e0. One 128 KB reply made the token scan read 2.05 billion characters to strip a single token. Leaked control tokens are a reported user-visible path (GLM-5 in #44179, the `<|...|>` leaks behind #40020), and any reply that quotes a token — tokenizer help, F#/Elm `<|` examples, documentation — takes the same code path. The sanitizer runs for every streamed reply on the single-threaded Gateway, so the repeated work delays session updates and channel deliveries while the reply streams.

## User Impact

Replies that contain or quote a control token now scan each appended delta once instead of re-running the whole-reply scrub. End to end, the streamed delivery projection drops from 5.6 s to 0.65 s of CPU at 65 KB and from 23.4 s to 2.2 s at 128 KB; the token scan itself drops from 528 M to 65 K characters at 65 KB and from 2.05 G to 128 K at 128 KB. Tilde-dense prose drops from 21.2 s to 0.64 s at 65 KB. Visible output is unchanged: tokens outside code are still removed, code examples are still preserved, and streamed deltas still concatenate to the batch result.

The one-pass bound covers token/backtick-sparse replies, which is the reported case. Inline-code-dense replies still revalidate once per backtick delta, because a backtick can change ownership of an earlier token; the cost is bounded by the number of backtick deltas, not every delta, and output stays exact. A follow-up could skip revalidation inside a settled fence. Other sanitizer stages are unchanged and keep their own pre-existing per-delta costs.

## Why This Change Was Made

`stripModelSpecialTokens()` was registered with `activationTokens`, so once any `<|`/`<｜` appeared every delta ran the canonical transform over the whole cumulative reply. The transform cannot settle the input because the leaked token remains in the source, so it also re-ran `findCodeRegions()` and the full match scan each time.

The filter now provides a projector that keeps the stripped output and appends a delta directly only when that delta cannot change the result: no token opener, no token split across the boundary, no pending separator after a token at the end, no surrogate-pair split after it, no backtick, and no 3+ tilde run (two characters are carried so a split fence opener still revalidates). Backtick and tilde-fence deltas are the only ones that can change code ownership, so they re-run the canonical transform and can emit a corrected replacement; everything else appends directly. Token boundaries are found from their pipes rather than the last `<`, so a token body containing `<` is handled too.

`transform` remains the canonical batch path, so history and delivery extraction are untouched.

## Evidence

Minimal repro (through the shipped `createAssistantVisibleStreamText()` projection, 4-character deltas, one `<|assistant|>` followed by ordinary prose), measured on Windows 11 / Node 26.11.1:

| Reply | Before: total / token-scan chars | After: total / token-scan chars |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 32 KB | 1,295 ms / 128,144,037 | 243 ms / 32,041 |
| 65 KB | 5,616 ms / 528,417,537 | 651 ms / 65,041 |
| 128 KB | 23,384 ms / 2,048,576,037 | 2,176 ms / 128,041 |

Output matched the batch result in every case (`matchesBatch: true`). A tilde-dense 65 KB reply (many `~12 ms`-style numbers) measured 21,223 ms before the tilde narrowing and 639 ms after, with the token scan at 65,041 characters.

Independent review found and this branch fixed four boundary problems across earlier heads:

- A token inside an inline code span whose closing backtick arrived after more text was stripped and never restored when the span closed. A backtick delta now re-runs the canonical transform, so the closing delta emits the corrected replacement.
- The first gate used the raw inline-code scanner, which treats a lone or escaped backtick as an open span forever and disabled the fast path for the rest of the reply (16 KB: 12.1 s). The gate now keys on the deltas that can change ownership: stray and escaped backticks cost one revalidation (16 KB: 58–76 ms) instead of disabling the fast path.
- The ownership gate matched any tilde delta, so tilde-dense prose paid a full scan per tilde. It now matches only 3+ tilde runs.
- A token that batch sanitization stripped inside a reference definition stayed stripped after a later suffix invalidated the definition (the image became unresolved and its code span became code-owned again), and the mirror case left a standalone definition label's token kept where batch strips it. The projector now keeps the token decision unsettled while a definition has no blank-line boundary after it - the same boundary the canonical parser uses for its stable-prefix rule - for tokens currently stripped and for kept tokens in a line-start label whose `]` is missing, is the last character, or is followed by `:`. Appends re-run the canonical transform until the definition settles.

Regression coverage in `src/shared/text/model-special-tokens.streaming.test.ts`:

- 37 fixtures × chunk sizes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 64 vs `stripModelSpecialTokens()` and delta accounting
- per-prefix parity: every 1-character prefix equals the batch transform of that prefix
- split opener, token at the end with a pending separator, replacement replay, inline-code ownership change, closer-run revocation, escaped backticks, tilde fences, token body containing `<`, astral and combining-mark boundaries, image-label revocation, and reference-definition settlement (strip, restore, and standalone-definition label cases)
- three bounded-work assertions (plain, stray backtick, tilde-dense prose): fewer than 4× the source length scanned by the token pattern, versus about 32 M characters on the pre-fix path for the 16 KB fixture

Checks run locally:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/shared/text/model-special-tokens.streaming.test.ts` — 49 passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run` on the filter consumers (`assistant-visible-text*`, `text-projection`, `strip-markdown`, `embedded-agent-utils.strip-model-special-tokens`) — all passed
- `pnpm tsgo:core` — exit 0
- cross-check fuzz: 4,000 randomly assembled markup sources × chunk sizes 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 16 (24,000 streamed runs) vs the batch transform — zero divergences
- `pnpm test test/scripts/eager-import-closure.test.ts` — 14 passed, 5 skipped
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check` on the three touched files — clean
- `pnpm exec oxlint --type-aware --config .oxlintrc.json` on the three touched files — 0 warnings, 0 errors
- `pnpm check:max-lines-ratchet` reports the three inherited `ui/` suppressions already present on the base commit; no `ui/` file is touched by this PR.

Only one problem is addressed. No configuration, migration, or dependency changes.

## AI disclosure

AI disclosure: this change was drafted with AI assistance at my request, under my direction and review. I set the scope (bounded incremental work with batch parity), required the before/after reproduction, and reviewed the code and evidence before opening this PR.

## Shipped Gateway behavior proof (2026-10-19)

Added after review. The streaming path is now exercised through a real `gateway run` process, not only the shared module, and the image-ownership finding has a base-failing / repaired-head-passing regression.

**65 KB reply that starts with a leaked `<|assistant|>` token, provider streaming four-character deltas** (16,254 SSE events in 3,332 ms from a local OpenAI-compatible fixture provider). Run against this head (`d0cf858d45a0`) through `gateway run`; Gateway process CPU sampled, control round subtracted.

```json
{
  "providerEvents": 16254, "providerEmitMs": 3332, "chunkChars": 4,
  "deliveredChars": 65000,
  "deliveredSha256": "28570f36dc0a15ff736fc4845448d73daccd4e8eb8e59a247fef4fe76483ce72",
  "deliveredDeltas": 51, "chatDeltas": 51,
  "deliveredHasRawToken": false, "deliveredDeltasHaveRawToken": false,
  "streamWindowMs": 3970, "firstDeltaMs": 553, "lastDeltaMs": 4523,
  "terminalStatus": "ok", "terminalMs": 4698,
  "gatewayCpuSec": 6.02, "controlCpuSec": 0.83, "streamingCpuSec": 5.19
}
```

The delivered 65,000 characters are byte-identical to the canonical batch transform of the source (`stripModelSpecialTokens()`), so streamed delivery and batch delivery agree exactly (stream sha and delivered sha verified against the source in-process).

<details><summary>Raw client transcript (redacted)</summary>

```text

[client] control turn completed in 652ms (gateway cpu delta 0.83s)

[client] delivered head: "The gateway keeps the session transcript and streams the rep"

```

</details>

**Ownership revocation (P2) regression now has a base-failing / head-passing pair.** Same test file, same command:

```text

  $ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/shared/text/model-special-tokens.streaming.test.ts
  Test Files  1 failed (1)
  Tests  8 failed | 28 passed (36)
    token inside an image label resolved by a late definition at 1 chars:
      expected '![a `<|assistant|>`][id]\n\n[id]: /ur…' to be '![a ``][id]\n\n[id]: /url\n'
    token inside an image label with an inline destination at 1 chars:
      expected '![a `<|assistant|>`](/img.png)\n' to be '![a ``](/img.png)\n'
    (plus inline title, shortcut label, definition-continuation, prefix-33, and the two dedicated revocation tests)
```

Also re-run on this head: cross-check fuzz (24,000 streamed variants vs the batch transform, including the image late-definition and inline-destination prefixes) with zero divergences, plus tsgo, type-aware lint, and format checks clean.

**Definition settlement (P2) regression now has a base-failing / head-passing pair.** Same test file, same command:

```text

    (plus the definition-title, next-line-destination, collapsed, shortcut, settled-paragraph, every-prefix, and two dedicated definition tests)
```

prs.title: fix(gateway): reject malformed usage cost scopes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Malformed `usage.cost` scope selectors can silently normalize to the default agent and return a report for a scope the caller did not request.

## Why This Change Was Made

The canonical `usage.cost` RPC owner rejects a provided non-string `agentId`, an unsupported `agentScope`, or an agent combined with `agentScope: "all"` before resolving the default owner or loading cost data. Standalone blank `agentId` remains equivalent to omission, including the existing blank-plus-all form; the earlier proposal to reject standalone blank values has been removed.

## User Impact

Malformed direct RPC requests receive `INVALID_REQUEST`. Valid default, explicit-agent, all-agent, standalone blank, and blank-plus-all requests retain their established behavior, including usage created by the installed stable release before upgrading.

## Evidence

- A [fresh comparison against pinned main](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/compare/9a5b671320277cac11a8b4c7be233668681e6362...03968fb877d0d77ec7e7cbaa50dfd74074792782) reports only **two contributor-changed files, +32/-3**: production `usage.ts` +17/-3 and the existing scope test +15/-0. The older 373-file PR metadata includes upstream commits brought by the main integration; it is not a list of contributor changes or conflicting files.
- A local three-way merge preview against this main found no conflict in the two-file patch. No merge, source rewrite or push was performed. Being behind main is not a reason by itself to invalidate and rerun the existing upgrade proof.
- The [latest durable review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/158696#issuecomment-5843840180) is marked stale for this head; no current-head rating is claimed. Existing CI also remains unresolved: [run 38352828050](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38352828050) failed a Bun `chat.native-runtime-consent.test.ts` case. That failure is recorded, not waived by the successful focused tests below.
- The [sensitive-change guard](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/158696#issuecomment-6139109946) was raised over the older expanded PR comparison and still requests maintainer approval. Its status remains authoritative until the repository reevaluates it. This update neither removes the guard nor claims that approval is unnecessary.

No CHANGELOG, temporary proof assets, dependency, config/default, protocol schema, authority, database migration or persistence format change is introduced.

- Limitations: controlled loopback model responses substitute for external inference; no interactive UI, actual provider account/authentication, external messaging, other OS, plugin-heavy configuration or full-range historical release migration is claimed. Existing explicit-owner authorization and unknown-agent handling remain intact. Hosted exact-head CI and durable rating are tracked separately.

prs.title: fix(gateway): report stt-tts readiness and transports in talk.catalog
prs.body:
Related: #165363 ## What Problem This Solves Android can reject a working native Talk setup because setup readiness is taken from an unrelated realtime provider, while `talk.catalog` does not expose selected-speech readiness and transport metadata. ## User Impact Configured native Talk can use device speech recognition and the selected speech provider without requiring a realtime provider. Existing device-TTS fallback is preserved for missing or unsupported speech providers; a selected, known provider without credentials still requires setup. Realtime Talk continues to use realtime readiness. No configuration migration, schema change, or new dependency is introduced. Physical-device/live-provider and fresh-install/latest-stable upgrade validation remain outstanding; the evidence below does not claim those flows have been tested. ## Why This Change Was Made - Derive `speech.ready` from the active speech row's asynchronous configured result and expose `managed-room` transport metadata. - Reuse Android's existing Talk route parser to select native-speech or realtime readiness. Native recognition does not depend on Gateway transcription readiness. - Invalidate setup readiness after configuration changes and reject stale refresh results. Label the shared setup row “Talk,” not “Realtime Talk.” - Regenerate the source-owned native localization inventory for the changed labels and configuration-error text. Translated catalogs and locale metadata remain owned by the localization workflow. Original implementation by @holny; Android route-readiness follow-up and CI correction contributed with @IWhatsskill. ## Work sessions - [Discussion, implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/dashboard/af8d6636-39eb-4922-8f37-2d4ba8a42bb8) ## Evidence ### Current localization follow-up Commit `7784d02a30ab425bfb75aef40a155ba778c3245a` changes only `apps/.i18n/native-source.json` (4 additions, 2 deletions), generated by `pnpm native:i18n:baseline`. - Reproduced the exact `native app i18n inventory drift detected` failure on `63959e26026939388010d16ca2b133d0b7a4891b` using `pnpm native:i18n:verify`. - After regeneration, `pnpm native:i18n:verify` passes, including Android and Apple source-localization checks; 4,483 inventory entries. - Repeated generation is byte-identical. Verification passes again after the commit; `git diff --check` passes. Local runtime: Node 26.8.2, repository-pinned pnpm 12.9.0, frozen-lockfile dependencies. ### Android behavior and review — retained evidence for 63959e260269393 The localization-only follow-up does not change these runtime/test sources. These are prior-commit results, not a new execution of the whole suite: - The new Android admission regression failed on unchanged pre-fix Android source, then passed with the route-aware fix. - **43 focused Android tests passed:** readiness 13; NodeRuntime admission/stale-result/publication 3; Settings 1; composer 8; config parsing 10; mode manager 3; speech client 5. The selected Gradle tests and Kotlin lint completed in 48 seconds. The new 11-case admission regression took 2.137 seconds; the stale-result regression took 0.058 seconds. These are measured local times, not estimated CI seconds. - Kotlin lint, scoped formatting, documentation-content checks, and whitespace checks passed. - Two independent Codex autoreview passes over the complete implementation candidate and relevant route/fallback/lifecycle context found no actionable P0–P2 issues. ClawSweeper's October 14 review of the same head also reports no code findings, with behavior proof still outstanding. - The earlier exact-parent Gateway handler [CI job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38561600537/job/115844560368) passed 107 tests. This is parent-head evidence, not a current-head Gateway rerun. ### Settings screenshots Actual production Compose Settings rendering in a test harness, using French, a narrow viewport, and large text. These images demonstrate the shared label change only; they do **not** demonstrate successful Talk startup or audio. “Non vérifié” means “Unverified”: the fixture is deliberately disconnected. “Parler” is the translated “Talk” label.
BeforeAfter
### Live `talk.catalog` runtime proof Both scenarios run against an isolated loopback Gateway (`gateway.mode=local`, `bind=loopback`, port 18899) on the candidate build, invoked as `openclaw gateway call talk.catalog --params '{}'`. Scenario A - active provider present, no credentials (`talk.provider=elevenlabs`, `talk.providers.elevenlabs={}`): ```json { "speech.ready": false, "speech.activeProvider": "elevenlabs", "elevenlabs.configured": false, "elevenlabs.transports": ["managed-room"], "elevenlabs.modes": ["stt-tts"] } ``` Scenario B - same active provider after adding credentials: ```json { "speech.ready": true, "speech.activeProvider": "elevenlabs", "elevenlabs.configured": true, "elevenlabs.transports": ["managed-room"], "elevenlabs.modes": ["stt-tts"] } ``` This is the readiness the fix derives from the active speech row: the selected, known provider reports `ready:false` (`configured:false`) without credentials, and `ready:true` once configured. A synthetic key was used and does not appear in the catalog output. ### CI failure disposition and remaining proof The [CI attempt for 63959e260269393](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38570885471) failed in two independent jobs: - `native-i18n`: missing source-inventory regeneration, corrected by the localization follow-up above. - `android-test-third-party`: downloading `gradle-9.7.1-bin.zip` returned HTTP 500 before tests started. This is not a passing test result or evidence of a code failure. Its downstream `openclaw/ci-gate` also failed. New-head hosted CI remains separate from the local passing check; no manual CI rerun or merge is claimed here. The live `openclaw gateway call talk.catalog` evidence above closes the earlier runtime-proof gap; physical-device native Talk startup/audio, device fallback and unchanged realtime admission, and fresh-install/latest-stable upgrade runs with settings preserved remain outstanding. No full repository suite was run locally.
Implementation history - The initial test-only commit `ca0f5eeaa0e` did not contain the production change; `2404bf77d27` supplied it. - `33df65b6c59a` preserved main's asynchronous provider-catalog structure and corrected selected-provider readiness for missing credentials. - `63959e260269393` added Android route-aware admission, fallback preservation, configuration-refresh protection, focused regressions, and the shared Talk label. The Android admission blocker is therefore no longer excluded from this PR's scope; live proof remains open as stated above.

prs.title: fix(gateway): settle restart resends canceled during preparation
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A startup resend interrupted after source registration but before content preparation returned could lose its cancellation receipt. Recovery then counted the canceled, unstarted turn as failed instead of settling it. The deterministic real-Gateway regression preserves the assertions for no resend model call, the terminal recovery marker, a successful replacement turn, and no replay on the next startup.

Cancellation publication now keeps the original admission check. If that check rejects because this request's own execution was canceled, a separate check requires its exact aborted source and still-current Gateway, caller, and operator policy before recording the receipt. Observed source-identity loss stays revoked. Normal execution and retained-tool authority remain unchanged.

The initial PR applied the exception too broadly: PR CI caught delayed public Stop receipts, an unauthorized media write, and lost cached replay during Gateway close. This revision restores those contracts. The pending-terminal publisher check applies only to the cancellation fallback; ordinary Stop keeps its immediate reservation receipt and existing media/join behavior. No restart-specific branch is added to the dedupe owner.

The conflicting execution-liveness check originated in #175837; the reported eleven-commit hourly window did not modify these owners. This change adds no schema, dependency, baseline, timeout, or retry change. It also removes an unnecessary internal preflight copy and supplies the existing authority assertion to the typed recovery test fixture.

## Evidence

- Deterministic negative control on `50520de188dd`: the controlled early-preparation ordering reproduces `failed: 1, settled: 0` rather than `failed: 0, settled: 1`. A later-preparation control passes, isolating the missing early receipt.
- Reproduced all three PR-CI sibling regressions on `18e58d6b60ec`: four failed cases across the upload-policy, metadata-read-authority, and late-admission files. The revised five-file focused run passes **38/38 tests** with `pnpm test <files> --maxWorkers=1` (162.93 s), including the original startup regression and exact-owner/policy-revocation checks.
- The full requested **366-file gateway-server-parallel selection** completed with four workers: **4,194 passed, 4 failed, 13 skipped** (2,514.61 s). All 18 cases across the four requested regression files passed under that load. No test assertions or timeout budgets changed.
- All seven consumers of the adjusted recovery fixture pass **239/239 tests** across the infra, agents-support, and isolated agent configs (`--maxWorkers=1`; 555.12 s). The two additional dedupe/currentness and persistence files also pass all **17 tests** with one worker.
- Gateway-server typecheck, targeted typed and boundary lint, formatting, and fresh staged-candidate P0–P2 autoreview pass. Final review is scoped-clean.

Local proof uses the repository wrappers and pinned Bun on macOS. No assertions were weakened, no CI job was rerun or dispatched, and landing remains with the lead.

The full run also exposed failures outside the changed cancellation path. A one-worker comparison of their four files passed all 19 cases on exact pre-PR source; the repaired source passed 18/19, with a different `agent.wait` shutdown variant hitting its existing five-second emergency-release assertion. The connected variant from the full run passed there. The remaining timing failure is in the unchanged `agent.wait`/shutdown path and is recorded without claiming it fixed. The pass-through cleanup, ACP routing, and required-placement cases passed on both sources.

A separate sidecar suite was blocked in the full run because the local compiled build stamp belonged to another commit. After rebuilding through the repository runtime owner, both sidecar cases passed. The runtime build itself passed for the repaired source. No full-suite or CI retry was used to seek a green result.

prs.title: feat(inworld): add speakingRate and deliveryMode options, list TTS-2 models
prs.body:
Related: #167950
Related: #77921 (original TTS-2 migration by @cshape; this PR adds the TTS-2 model ids and request options without changing the default)

### What Problem This Solves
Inworld voices can only play at their native pace, and on `inworld-tts-2` the delivery control the API provides (`deliveryMode`, which per Inworld's API reference is used in place of `temperature` on that model) is not exposed; the TTS-2 model ids are missing from the model list.

### User Impact
User impact: operators can set `tts.providers.inworld.speakingRate` (0.5–1.5) to slow down or speed up Inworld speech for replies, Talk and telephony, pick `deliveryMode` (`STABLE`, `BALANCED`, `CREATIVE`) for `inworld-tts-2`, override speaking rate per message with `[[tts:speed=…]]` and per Talk request with the existing `speed` parameter, override delivery per message with `[[tts:delivery=…]]`, and select `inworld-tts-2` / `inworld-tts-2-flash` from the model list. The default model and existing `temperature` behavior are unchanged. Per Inworld's API reference, `deliveryMode` is honored only by `inworld-tts-2` and ignored on other models, including `inworld-tts-2-flash`; the docs and manifest say so.

### Why This Change Was Made
Follows the guidance on #77921: fresh branch on current main, narrow scope, pinned legacy ids preserved, current response-size/timeout/parsing/base64 hardening untouched, no vendor attribution header, default unchanged. The Inworld TTS request already builds an `audioConfig`; this adds the optional `speakingRate` field there and the top-level `deliveryMode`, and plumbs both through the provider config, Talk config and the directive parser. Talk per-call overrides consume the existing `talk.speak` `speed` parameter (mapped to `speakingRate`), matching the OpenAI provider; there is no per-call `deliveryMode` because `TalkSpeakParamsSchema` does not carry it. The manifest schema bounds `speakingRate` (0.5–1.5) and enumerates `deliveryMode`, so config validation rejects other values; directive values outside the range or set are ignored with a warning, matching the existing `temperature` handling.

Config surface: the two new optional plugin keys raise the plugin config-doc budget from 4600 to 4602 on rebased head f096cbc (`docs/.generated/config-baseline.counts.json` and `.sha256` regenerated with `pnpm config:docs:gen`). Both keys are operator controls that map 1:1 to documented Inworld request fields; neither has a sensible derived default.

### Evidence
- `pnpm test:extension inworld`: on rebased head f096cbc, 3 files, 33 tests passed (the separate 2026.10.3 proof build below ran 37/37 with 10.3's extra defaults test). Coverage: request body carries `audioConfig.speakingRate` and `deliveryMode` (and omits `deliveryMode` when unset); provider config and Talk config for both; Talk `speed` → `speakingRate` mapping, including an out-of-range `speed` dropped; directive parsing for both; out-of-range `speakingRate` and unknown `deliveryMode` dropped from config resolution; invalid directive values warn; the voice-settings directive policy is respected.
- Test cost (`pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`): `speech-provider.test.ts` 1.7 s wall, `tts.test.ts` 5.8 s wall; no timers, sleeps or process boots added.
- `pnpm config:docs:check` OK; `pnpm plugins:inventory:check` OK; oxlint and oxfmt clean; `pnpm tsgo:extensions:all` clean.
- Current-stable **v2026.10.4 configuration preservation** is also tested: released 10.4 (`383c124`) with official stock Inworld 2026.10.4 → the same persisted state on recorded main `956d410` → exact PR archive `1f6fc01`. Complete nonsecret Inworld/Talk settings snapshots are byte-identical at each stage, the installed runtime hashes match the reviewed archive, and Gateway activation/readback plus provider config resolution pass. No key or synthesis was used. Final activation uses the recorded main build because the released 10.4 core lacks the shared parser export; this is not a direct released-core plugin compatibility claim. Reviewed current-stable follow-up: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/167951#issuecomment-6231682178

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Real behavior proof (authenticated, redacted)

Run on 2026-10-09 against this PR head (`14e77e99993`) with the plugin's own `synthesize` / `synthesizeTelephony` / `resolveTalkOverrides` hooks through `openclaw/plugin-sdk/plugin-test-runtime`, hitting the live Inworld API with a real key (header redacted). The request bodies below are the exact JSON the plugin sent; durations are computed from the returned 22.05 kHz 16-bit PCM.

- Case A: operator config `speakingRate: 1.3` + `deliveryMode: "CREATIVE"` on `inworld-tts-2` → request carries `audioConfig.speakingRate: 1.3` and top-level `deliveryMode: "CREATIVE"`, HTTP 200, MP3 returned.

## Shipped-flow proof on latest stable (2026-10-14, redacted)

Isolated, clean OpenClaw **2026.10.3** gateway (official container image `ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.10.3`, fresh state, no channels). Inworld key held as a store SecretRef. Request bodies were captured with `openclaw proxy run`; the credential header is redacted by the capture layer and none appears below. Same sentence every time.

**1. Upgrade from latest stable, existing settings intact**
- Installed the published `@openclaw/inworld-speech@2026.10.3`, configured as an existing user would: `voiceId: "Ashley"`, `modelId: "inworld-tts-1.5-max"`, `temperature: 0.8`. `infer tts convert` through the gateway returned audio (5.42 s).
- Installed this PR's build over it (2026.10.3 + this PR's two code commits, plugin `2026.10.3+deltawerks.f096cbc`), then restarted the gateway.
- On restart, core 2026.10.3 doctor moved `voiceId` → `speakerVoiceId`. That migration is core's, not this PR's. The value survived, and the request after upgrade is unchanged apart from field placement:
  `{"voiceId":"Ashley","modelId":"inworld-tts-1.5-max","audioConfig":{"audioEncoding":"MP3"},"temperature":0.8}`. HTTP 200, 5.33 s. No `speakingRate` or `deliveryMode` is sent when they aren't configured.

**2. Config loading (`speakingRate`)**: `config set tts.providers.inworld.speakingRate 1.25` (applied live, no restart) →
  `{"voiceId":"Ashley","modelId":"inworld-tts-1.5-max","audioConfig":{"audioEncoding":"MP3","speakingRate":1.25},"temperature":0.8}`. HTTP 200, 3.91 s vs 5.33 s.

**3. `deliveryMode` on `inworld-tts-2`**: `modelId: "inworld-tts-2"`, `deliveryMode: "CREATIVE"` →

prs.title: feat(agents): expose gateway health to the system agent
prs.body:
Closes #171971

## What Problem This Solves

The system agent's direct `openclaw` tool rejects `{ action: "health" }` as an unknown action, even though OpenClaw already owns a canonical read-only `health` operation, parser entry, and executor. Operators cannot ask the setup and repair assistant whether the Gateway is healthy, or which channels are degraded, in the same turn through the model-facing tool.

## Why This Change Was Made

Register `health` in the direct tool's `SYSTEM_AGENT_TOOL_ACTIONS` schema enum and `SIMPLE_ACTIONS` map so it maps to the existing canonical `{ kind: "health" }` operation with `approved: false`, advertise it in the tool description, and align the primary direct-tool system prompt's read-action list to include `health`. The existing executor calls `healthCommand` and returns the canonical health projection. The canonical chain — operation (`operation-types.ts`), parser (`operations-parse.ts`), executor (`operations-execute.ts` → `healthCommand`) — is untouched; only the tool entry, its test, the description, and the prompt read-action list change. No configuration, persisted schema, migration, probe implementation, or write authority changes. Same shape as the merged #133255 (`plugin_list`).

## User Impact

The system agent can read overall Gateway health and per-channel status in the same turn, through the same model-facing entry. Existing `gateway_status`, `status`, search, install/uninstall, and approval behavior remain unchanged. Health reads do not perform repairs.

## Evidence

Base: `cbc9f479397` (origin/main). Contributor head: `de61f3323d8c`.

**Focused tests** — `system-agent-tool.test.ts`: 20 passed. The `health` row asserts caller-visible boundaries — `health` is present in the tool's schema enum and advertised in its description as a free read.

**Prompt snapshots** — `generate-prompt-snapshots.ts --check`: 7 files current.

**Shipped-MCP-process proof** — The shipped MCP server entry point (`src/mcp/openclaw-tools-serve.ts`) is launched as a child process via `StdioClientTransport`. A real MCP SDK `Client` connects over stdio. A real `startGatewayServer` runs on a fixed port with token auth. No mock of `operations.js`; no approval proposal staged.

| Check | Pre-fix (health removed) | Post-fix (head `de61f3323d`) |
|-------|--------------------------|------------------------------|
| `tools/list` exposes `openclaw` | present | present |
| action enum contains `health` | FAIL — 35 items, position -1 | PASS — 36 items, position 8 |
| `tools/call { action: "health" }` | FAIL — `unknown action "health"` | PASS — real health snapshot, no approval |
| unknown action still rejected | PASS | PASS — `{ isError: true }`, `unknown action` |

Post-fix `tools/call` readback (redacted) — a real Gateway health snapshot from the shipped MCP process:

```
Gateway event loop: ok max=21ms p99=21ms util=0.014 cpu=1.749
Gateway check duration: 27829ms
Agents: dev
Heartbeat interval: 30m (dev)
Session store (dev): <state>/agents/dev/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite (0 entries)
```

Removing `health` from the enum and `SIMPLE_ACTIONS` map reproduces the pre-fix `unknown action` rejection, so the proof guards the behavior change in both directions.

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. `Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Per review, the proof now launches the shipped MCP server as a child process via `StdioClientTransport` and returns a real health snapshot from a running Gateway.

prs.title: fix(macos): use shared exec policy with PostgreSQL
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes native exec approvals using the wrong policy owner when PostgreSQL is selected. The Mac still opened `state/openclaw.sqlite`, which is only the engine anchor on PostgreSQL installations. SQLite installations had separate Swift and TypeScript writers of the same policy.

Step 0 exercised the actual pre-change Swift store on synthetic roots at base `7e8d1f08c151d1c029319093bfde0ca0d8ba3572`. SQLite read/write succeeded and created/updated `exec_approvals_config`. With PostgreSQL selected and a canonical anchor, both calls refused with `Schema version zero database contains objects not owned by a native OpenClaw store`. The anchor retained only `openclaw_engine_anchor`; Swift never reached PostgreSQL policy. This is an ownership gap, not evidence of anchor corruption.

## User Impact

Native execution, the local CLI, and Gateway enforcement now use one shared exec policy on both engines. Policy unavailability denies execution with a diagnostic; there is no direct database or cached-policy fallback. Existing headless enforcement and per-node `exec.approvals.node.get/set` routing remain in place.

No schema migration is needed. Socket credentials remain with the local credential owner introduced in #174599; the typed owner adapter follows the runtime-pin precedent in #172703.

## Why This Change Was Made

The native adapter calls bounded get, expected-hash replace, and authorization-commit operations through the existing local-state owner route. A running owner receives the request; otherwise the CLI takes exclusive offline custody with the selected engine. The Swift shared-policy SQL store, migration gate, duplicate mutation logic, and obsolete tests are removed.

The native final commit semantically re-authorizes against the current effective policy inside the locked write transaction, including current deny, invalid delayed policy, tightened security/ask, removed submitted matches, revoked skill auto-allow, and the agent-deletion fence. Policy edits that keep this command allowed do not deny it; execution deliberately does not require raw-JSON hash equality, because usage metadata also changes that hash. Usage/allow-always grants are recorded under the same writer admission. It is awaited within the original native socket request. On return, native checks cancellation and enqueues without another suspension; immediately before spawn it checks the bound executable (including original dispatch resolution), cwd, and Gateway-derived skill trust. Executable/cwd/env binding stays native-side; the unused duplicate `execution` wire payload is removed. No transaction spans IPC, and no bearer token, polling, revocation generation, or distributed handshake is introduced. Cancellation after a durable commit may leave recorded usage/grants, but cannot use the response to spawn.

Update behavior:

- An older app still admitted on SQLite addresses the same policy row. It does not gain PostgreSQL support; the existing refusal of retired credential access remains in force.
- A new app with an older CLI or owner missing the required operation denies with a diagnostic. It never opens the database as a fallback.
- Rollback retains the unchanged policy schema. Use an app/CLI combination compatible with current data; do not restore stale permissions or rewind local credentials. The old native direct-file implementation remains unsupported with PostgreSQL.

## Evidence

- Owner contract tests cover SQLite and PostgreSQL: snapshot redaction, expected-hash replacement/stale refusal, grants/usage, real persistence failure and rollback, agent deletion, offline custody, and unavailable-owner denial.
- Existing owner routing (36), Gateway authority/handlers (22), protocol (8), and authorization worker (5) tests pass.
- Coordinator follow-up: all 6 native semantic-regression cases pass on SQLite/PostgreSQL through the production evaluator, current owner commit and native executor: matched-rule removal and deny prevent spawn; unrelated-rule removal still spawns. The test does not put extra owner calls inside a single bounded transport request.
- Coordinator follow-up: 76 touched TypeScript cases pass, including both engines, owner routing, Gateway authority and protocol validation. All 31 affected native-bootstrap/Doctor migration cases pass after freezing the historical v0 fixture schema. That fixture had derived its four old tables from current Swift, so deleting Swift policy SQL produced an independently reproduced `3 != 4` setup failure. No application migration code or schema changed.
- Native boundary proof on the reviewed follow-up covers 8 tests / 18 cases. prs.title: fix(native-hook-relay): rearm relay expiry on monotonic clock
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A native hook relay keeps host policy active for its TTL. Its in-process expiry rearm timer computed remaining time as `expiresAtMs - Date.now()`. Both are **wall-clock**, so a backward system clock jump (NTP sync, manual clock set) inflates `remainingMs` and the relay **lingers long past its TTL**, holding retained host policy/authority beyond its intended lifetime.

- Problem: the in-process rearm timer mixed a wall-clock seed (`expiresAtMs`) with a wall-clock consume (`Date.now()`), so relay expiry was not monotonic and a backward clock jump deferred unregistration.
- Solution: keep `expiresAtMs` as the cross-process wall-clock epoch shared through the bridge record, and add a process-local monotonic deadline `expiresAtMonotonicMs` (`performance.now() + ttl`) consumed only by the in-process rearm timer.
- What changed:
  - `native-hook-relay-types.ts` — the new `expiresAtMonotonicMs` lives in the **private** `RelayLifetime`, never exposed through the SDK handle.
  - `native-hook-relay.ts` — the rearm loop reads the monotonic deadline from the private lifetime; `register` and `renew` both set it.
  - Regression test in `native-hook-relay.test.ts`.
- What did NOT change: the cross-process epoch comparisons (`Date.now() > expiresAtMs`) and the CLI's local monotonic deadline remain untouched. Forward wall-clock jumps are not claimed; the change targets the in-process rearm timer only.

## Why This Change Was Made

Best fix: yes. Mirrors the dual-clock pattern merged for the same wall-clock family in #168731 (`inference-proxy.ts`: keep the epoch for the cross-domain contract, add a parallel `performance.now()` deadline for in-process `setTimeout` consumers). `expiresAtMs` cannot be replaced wholesale with `performance.now()` — it is persisted into the SQLite bridge record and compared against `Date.now()` by client/worker/store processes.

Rejected: the naive swap of `expiresAtMs` to `performance.now()` entirely (as the bug-tracker entry proposed) — it would break the cross-process epoch contract.

Risk / boundaries: the cross-process epoch comparisons stay on the wall clock and out of scope. `renew` updates both fields together; the rearm loop falls back to `expiresAtMs` only if a registration lacks the monotonic deadline.

## User Impact

Native hook relays now expire at exactly their configured TTL regardless of a **backward** wall-clock jump (NTP sync or manual clock set), so operators no longer see native relays linger and hold host policy/authority past their expiry when the machine clock is corrected backward. Cross-process expiry behavior is unchanged.

## Evidence

Live authority-chain proof with the **real HTTP bridge + a separately launched relay CLI subprocess** (no mocks): the relay owner runs in-process against the real bridge HTTP server; the client is a **separate cold process** running the built relay CLI entry (`node dist/native-hook-relay/entry.js hooks relay --state-db <sqlite>`), spawned via `child_process` over real pipes, talking to the owner's bridge through the persisted bridge record in SQLite. Scripts live under the PR author's evidence directory.

### Before / after (the fix's one real difference)

Same setup on both sides, only the rearm source differs. Backward wall-clock rollback **600,000 ms** right after a 20s-TTL relay registers:

| | Before fix (`expiresAtMs - Date.now()`) | After fix (monotonic `expiresAtMonotonicMs`) |
|---|---|---|
| Relay at TTL+800ms | **`registered = true` — LINGERED** | **`registered = false` — EXPIRED on time** |
| Separate CLI subprocess after TTL | relay still held, unregistered late | returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` (revoked) |

```console
# Before fix
after TTL+800ms (wall clock still rolled back), registered = true
RESULT: LINGERED past TTL (backward clock rollback bug present)

# After fix
after TTL+800ms (wall clock still rolled back), registered = false
RESULT: EXPIRED on time despite backward clock rollback (monotonic fix works)
RESULT2: independent CLI subprocess DENIED after expiry (authority revoked)
```

Before the fix the relay holds host policy/authority long past its TTL when the clock is corrected backward; after the fix it expires at exactly its TTL and the CLI is denied.

### Authority-chain integrity (passes on both sides, confirms relay semantics)

Separate CLI subprocess reaches the retained child's `runBeforeToolCall` policy and is allowed before expiry; after TTL the relay is gone and the subprocess is denied:

```console
=== PRE-EXPIRY ===
exit: 0                              # retained child policy ran and was allowed
policyCalls: [ 'pre-tool-use' ]      # retained child hook policy actually executed
=== POST-EXPIRY (after TTL) ===
registered after TTL: false          # relay unregistered on schedule
exit: 0
stdout: {"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","permissionDecision":"deny","permissionDecisionReason":"Native hook relay unavailable"}}
policyCalls: [ 'pre-tool-use' ]      # no new policy call after expiry
```

A pending in-flight policy settles as **REVOKED** after the relay expires (the in-flight policy does not release authority):

```console
[probe] t~ policy in flight; signal.aborted = false | registered = true
[probe] t=TTL+ settled = null | signal.aborted = false | registered = false   # relay expired while policy still pending
[probe] policy onResolution called: cancelled                                 # pending callback settles AFTER expiry as revoked
{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","permissionDecision":"deny","permissionDecisionReason":"Native hook relay unavailable"}}
[RESULT] pending policy REVOKED after expiry (final-effect verified)
[RESULT2] independent CLI subprocess DENIED after expiry
```

### Regression test

`native-hook-relay.test.ts` "rearms relay expiry on monotonic time despite a wall-clock ±300000 ms jump" uses `vi.useFakeTimers()` + `vi.setSystemTime()` to distort the wall clock without touching monotonic time, then advances past TTL and asserts the relay is unregistered.

- Post-fix: full file passes — `Tests 63 passed (63)`.
- Pre-fix (rearm reverted to `expiresAtMs - Date.now()`, test kept): the backward-jump case fails because the relay lingers.

`native-hook-relay.lifecycle.test.ts` passes (27/27), confirming registration/renew/ownership paths are unaffected.

**Not tested**: a forward wall-clock jump crossing the cross-process epoch checks (out of scope); live end-to-end with an actual OS clock change (rollback is simulated by overriding `Date.now()` in the owner process).

**Open PR collision check**: no open PR touches `src/agents/harness/native-hook-relay*.ts`. No duplicate.

Private operations with a single production caller carry exported helpers, argument packets, and import indirection instead of living with the operation that owns them.

prs.title: fix(codex): restore session replies after native child recovery
prs.body:
Related: #176602

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Codex-backed session replies failing with `Plugin state authority is unavailable` while previously completed native children are being restored.

## User Impact

Sessions can finish recovery and reply without colliding with their own pending binding writes. Saved child results continue through the existing recovery path. No configuration or schema migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Restoration can enqueue binding writes and return before those writes settle. The next assignment read, or the ownership check immediately after monitor readiness, then correctly refuses the still-pending binding.

Wait on the existing submission and assignment queues between restoration phases, before subsequent assignment reads, and before resolving readiness. Authority checks, write receipts, and uncertain-outcome handling remain unchanged. This complements #176602: that change scopes unrelated writes; these writes belong to the binding being recovered.

## Evidence

- The two-child registered-monitor regression fails on the original code when recovery reads while the first restored assignment write is held. With this fix, both children restore and readiness waits for settlement.
- All **83 relevant tests pass**: 36 inventory tests plus 47 monitor, completion-delivery, and cancellation tests. Final inventory wall time: 15.57 s (about 3.8 s test execution); consumer wall time: 43.37 s including cold compilation.
- Targeted Codex plugin typecheck, type-aware lint, formatting, and diff checks pass. The plugin runtime rebuild passes.
- Live verification through the originally failing Gateway session: two consecutive successful replies after deploying the final rebuilt plugin, with no plugin-state authority or pending-assignment reconciliation warnings during verification.
- Independent review of the complete diff and supporting ownership/queue source found no actionable P0–P2 issues.

Proof limits: the regression runs the production monitor and binding mutation logic with an in-memory binding backing, controlled native responses, and a held write. The live checks exercised session recovery and replies; they were not an exhaustive native-subagent workload or an exactly-once delivery test. Hosted CI for `d4786e6bf15a32da6a1d9cc5d81909346df743c2` is green, including `openclaw/ci-gate`.

Session, run, and child identifiers are replaced consistently with aliases; paths, endpoints, credentials, model identities, and unrelated message content are omitted. This is extracted evidence, not a new synthetic run or a complete transcript.


prs.title: feat(plugins): expose requester-bound native delegation
prs.body:
Related: #175275

## What Problem This Solves

Plugins handling normal reply dispatch need a supported way to delegate to native children and collect results without replacing the requester's execution or permission context.

## User Impact

Eligible plugins can use optional `api.runtime.subagent.native.spawn` and `collect` while retaining the requester's identity, parent incarnation, model policy, finalized tool admission, and sandbox restrictions. Existing background helpers and ordinary noncollector spawning are unchanged. This capability is limited to normal Gateway `reply_dispatch`; detached callbacks, timers, direct ACP dispatch, and unsupported runtimes do not gain it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The facade reuses native spawning, collector ownership, and replay handling instead of adding a scheduler or privileged plugin identity. Identical in-flight requests join; mismatches fail. Tool hooks still run, with reserved native collector/replay parameters checked before effects. Host-only collector context is bound to its exact invocation so nested ordinary waits retain their own requester.

The sandbox follow-up passes the existing prepared sandbox policy into capability admission. Both configured sandbox restrictions and persisted required-sandbox restrictions now apply to native **spawn and collection**. Denied operations cannot use the facade to bypass the existing tool policy; allowed sandbox operations and unsandboxed controls still work.

The qualification follow-up also includes Peter Steinberger's upstream snapshot call-site fix from c711c071ed51dc5475d512635794ebd2748f3b51: remove an unsupported argument to the BigInt-stat helper, clearing the compiler/declaration blocker without changing runtime behavior.

## Evidence

**Draft: required non-draft CI and integrated-current-base validation remain unproved. This is not merge-ready.**

- **111 distinct SDK behavioral cases:** 61 freshly passed production-boundary cases, including four sandbox regressions; 50 unchanged, source-bound passing cases reused (34 collector, 7 reply-dispatch, 4 registry, 5 runtime-context). The four focused sandbox cases failed against the previous production adapter and passed after this fix. They are included in 61, not counted twice.
- The sandbox tests exercise the real reply dispatcher, finalized native tools, and native session/collector implementation. They cover configured and persisted-required sandbox policies for spawn and collection, plus allowed and unsandboxed controls. Only embedded model I/O is mocked. Prior veto, replay, revocation, empty-scope, rewrite, and nested-requester regressions remain covered.
- **77 separate snapshot/backup tests passed**, with **2 Windows-only skips**, reused unchanged for the sandbox-only follow-up.
- **Current compiler/build qualification passed:** core typecheck, all **29 selected default core-test compiler graphs**, and full `pnpm build`, including declarations and UI build. The actual plugin-SDK compiler graph includes the SDK contract test. No additional root/extension-specific compiler graphs are claimed; the separate type-only Vitest execution is not counted as behavioral or compiler proof.
- Changed-file formatting and typed lint passed. The complete current changed-check ran **all 37 stages: 35 passed, 2 failed**. Remaining failures are unchanged UI max-lines suppressions and unrelated dead exports. Their diagnostic source files match the original base; these failures remain **red and unwaived**, not a successful full baseline build or an integrated-current-base CI result.
- Full touched-source/test audits and all three independent API-only review partitions completed. The raw latest review reported one issue; direct source inspection disproved it (the inbound authority resolver returns flat fields, unlike the separate nested overlay helper). No supported actionable findings remain after adjudication; this is **not a raw-clean helper result**. Reviewers inspected source and receipts, not runtime tests.

<details>
<summary>Current qualification commands and limitations</summary>

```text
pnpm tsgo:core
# exit 0

pnpm tsgo:core:test
# exit 0; all 29 selected default graphs, including plugin-sdk

pnpm build
# exit 0; including declarations and UI build

node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn.production-boundary.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 --reporter=verbose
# exit 0; 61 passed

node scripts/check-changed.mjs --staged --base 65609329cfbf32427aa52b252d342b4537c39976 --timed
# exit 1; 35/37 stages passed, 2 unchanged failures as described above
```

Runtime checks used isolated state, configuration, and temporary directories; the resolved update-handoff database was verified private before execution. No live deployment or runtime configuration was changed. Historical failed and cancelled attempts are not counted as passes. No integrated-current-base CI or native landing admission is claimed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Removes private Gateway implementation selectors and unread options that production callers never vary.

## User Impact

No user-visible change. Gateway protocol fields, Plugin SDK contracts, config keys, persisted data, authorization, startup/shutdown settlement, and the standalone session-memory backend remain unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Startup, metadata, board, and Control UI handlers already use one implementation in production. Call those existing owners directly and let tests mock the owners instead of threading optional dependency bags. Also remove an orphaned queue filter and an unused lazy-import wrapper option.

This is the Gateway/core-owner area of a wider 135-path cleanup, split for CI attribution. Net production reduction: **190 lines**; test/support growth: **67 lines**, across 39 paths, including one removed mock-baseline exception. Test migrations stay below the production reduction.

## Best-effort tradeoffs accepted

- Startup migration no longer accepts unused detector/resolver/reconciliation replacements. #95699 and #108851 are active completed features, not dormant injection foundations. Registered-database admission, deletion discovery, validation, error settlement, and lazy reconciliation remain.
- Startup orchestration and deferred update checks no longer accept alternate implementations that no production caller supplied. #175989 already moved fixtures to canonical module mocks. The #150629 deferred lifecycle, awaited lazy imports, synchronous owner construction, readiness, and shutdown joins remain.
- Config issue summaries use their actual five-issue/root-normalized policy instead of an unused cap option and its finite-clamp branch. All seven production callers already use that policy. The #75060 recovery diagnostics fixed in #75081, terminal sanitization, and hidden counts remain.
- Chat metadata and board handlers no longer accept test-only dependency bags. Canonical owner availability, account/config identity, approval and effect checks, caching, cancellation, and actual persistence remain. The #118846 saturation fix and the board features from #111218/#111687 are retained.
- Control UI handlers no longer select alternative private loaders through a state-free factory. Existing lazy facades, exact source/target bindings, live read authority, and main's newer native Git owner remain. The features from #100434/#148070 are unchanged.
- Startup auth hydration no longer accepts a test-only dependency promise. The real #151074 startup repair remains: four parallel lazy imports, current config capture afterward, directory deduplication, scoped discovery, noninteractive read-only policy, and per-agent warnings.
- Queue-size filtering is deleted only because #175837 completed its caller migration. The original #167844 starvation fix remains in the migrated controller; FIFO, cancellation, capacity, replacement identity, and whole-lane counts remain.

prs.title: fix(buzz): preserve literal credential-file paths
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `--credential-file` silently changes quoted paths containing surrounding whitespace, reading the wrong credential file when a trimmed-name neighbor exists.

## User Impact

User impact: the Buzz QA adapter reads the exact `--credential-file` path supplied by the operator. Whitespace-only options still fail, and the default file-without-source detection still works.

## Why This Change Was Made

The adapter used `.trim()` on the credential file path before passing it to `readBuzzQaCredentialFile`, which reads via native `fs.readFile`. A path like `" /secure/buzz-qa.json "` was silently shortened to `"/secure/buzz-qa.json"`. Use the existing `readNonBlankString` to reject blank input while preserving the original path, consistently with the runtime's literal-path behavior for `--message-file` and `--command` options.

## Evidence

Product head: `7e6a1d21cb9d`; RED base: `919fcc263201`.

Adapter boundary regression in `adapter.runtime.test.ts` creates two real credential files (`buzz.json` and ` buzz.json ` with distinguishable roomIds) and verifies `createBuzzQaTransportAdapter` reads the literal whitespace-named file (pre-fix `.trim()` reads the neighbor, post-fix `readNonBlankString` reads the literal).

```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/buzz/src/qa/adapter.runtime.test.ts extensions/buzz/src/qa/credentials.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

| Scenario | Base (`.trim()`) | Head (`readNonBlankString`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `credentialFile: " buzz.json "` through shipped CLI | reads `buzz.json` (trimmed neighbor) | reads ` buzz.json ` (literal) |
| `credentialFile: "   "` | throws (blank rejected) | throws (blank rejected) |
| `credentialFile: "private/buzz-qa.json"` | correct path | correct path |

✨ Terminal screenshot showing shipped CLI behavior diff (base vs head) through `openclaw qa buzz --credential-file " buzz-creds.json "`:

![buzz-cli-proof](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SunnyShu0925/openclaw/proof-screenshot-172283/.proof-assets/buzz-cli-proof.png)

Real shipped CLI proof (head, `openclaw qa buzz --credential-file " buzz-creds.json "`). Only the literal file ` buzz-creds.json ` exists (no neighbor). The adapter reads it successfully and fails at relay connection:

```text
$ openclaw qa buzz --credential-file " buzz-creds.json " --provider-mode mock-openai
QA suite report: .artifacts/qa-e2e/suite-mv92z15o-99192496/qa-suite-report.md
QA suite summary: Channel transport canary: fail — connection failed (relay unreachable)
```

Real shipped CLI proof (base, pre-fix `.trim()`). The same command trims ` buzz-creds.json ` to `buzz-creds.json`, which does not exist:

```text
$ openclaw qa buzz --credential-file " buzz-creds.json " --provider-mode mock-openai
QA suite report: .artifacts/qa-e2e/suite-mv92zt8p-3d9c4c2a/qa-suite-report.md
QA suite summary: Channel transport canary: fail — Unable to read Buzz QA credential file /home/code/github/openclaw/buzz-creds.json. | ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/home/code/github/openclaw/buzz-creds.json'
```

The base error path shows `buzz-creds.json` (trimmed) instead of ` buzz-creds.json ` (literal), proving the bug. The head version reads the literal file successfully.

Validation: 13 passed (2 files), Vitest 5.5s. `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint`, `check-test-types` (extensions.test shard) passed.

Scope: 2 files; production +2/-1, tests +20/-27. No config, protocol, schema, permission, dependency or upgrade changes.

Not tested: real Buzz relay connections, Windows trailing-space filenames, or the complete repository suite.

prs.title: feat: retain configured fallbacks for opted-in session models
prs.body:
Related: #84865

## What Problem This Solves

Operators need to prefer one model for a conversation without losing their configured fallback chain when that model is unavailable.

## User Impact

Users can explicitly opt a selected session model into configured fallback, and operators can prioritize already-configured backup models for each selected model. Existing strict selections remain strict by default; model locks and caller-owned fallback lists keep their current behavior. Choosing another model normally, or clearing the policy, also withdraws the opt-in from turns that are already queued, waiting for admission or being retried after a live model switch, and from a fallback chain that is already running. A live switch that withdraws the opt-in makes the remaining retries strict even when the turn was admitted on the default, and a return to the default restores the default's configured fallbacks.

Opt-in can send the conversation to another configured provider and incur that provider's costs. Older versions do not implement the session policy and reject the new `fallbackPriority` metadata. Before downgrading, clear the session policy and remove that metadata, or restore the pre-feature config/state backup. This PR does not add an update-validation bypass.

## Why This Change Was Made

`sessions.patch` accepts `modelFallbackPolicy: "configured"` with an explicit selected model. Fallback does not replace the requested preference or write agent/global model defaults, including when the requested model is the agent's own default. A normal subsequent model selection is strict again; `modelFallbackPolicy: null` clears the opt-in. Explicit opt-in adopts the current selection as the session preference, including agent-originated selections, and clears a pending first-failure rollback to the previous model.

The policy belongs to the selection, so every existing selection owner carries or withdraws it together with the route: queued follow-ups, the admission fence, live model-switch retries and attempt recovery. A policy-only change uses the existing pending-switch marker. When a live switch grants or withdraws the opt-in, the shared fallback runner returns it to the outer retry owner, which rebuilds the candidate chain before another provider is tried; a switch that keeps the policy keeps the existing in-chain redirect. Cron passes its session row's policy only as the comparison value for live-switch detection; cron fallback lists stay job-owned and absolute.

Optional `fallbackPriority` metadata reorders only candidates already present in the effective configured chain. It cannot introduce a route or reorder an explicit caller list, including an empty list. It uses existing selection, persistence, queue, fallback and compaction owners rather than provider-specific pairings.

This addresses the resilience need in #84865 through an opt-in alternative. Unlike #120299, it does not restore fallback for every user pin. Maintainer acceptance of the explicit opt-in policy is still needed before merge.

## Evidence

- The first ClawSweeper review (`878d39db`) found three selection-propagation defects and the related security concern. `b6b787ab` fixed the queued follow-up and admission findings and made both outer retry owners apply the policy. The second review (`b6b787ab`) found that the shared fallback runner could still continue the old candidate chain after a consent change, plus a late sticky-write gap. Commit `3843d5ca` fixes both. Each fix has a regression test that failed before the fix.
- The third review (`8f408dd7`) found a late P1 with a security hold: the reply retry owner applied a live switch's route and policy but kept the admitted turn's `hasSessionModelOverride` and `modelOverrideSource`, so a policy-only withdrawal on a turn admitted on the default left the configured chain eligible, and a return to the default kept a pin's strictness. `d6ee8ef5` carries the committed selection's override status and source with the live selection and applies them with the policy; the regression cases for both transitions failed before the fix and pass with it (see the table and the test runs).
- Current `main` (`f13b3cd209c`) is merged into the branch (merge commit `8f408dd7`, no rebase). The earlier merge `f71df2ab` (main `d220cac2b74`) brought #168893, which lets a `before_model_resolve` hook replace a run's fallback chain at the run-entry boundary. Four production files conflicted with it (the command attempt and its parameter type, the run-entry types that main moved to `run-entry.types.ts`, and the cron executor); they now take the candidate chain from run-entry as main does and keep this PR's policy and provenance fields. A hook-supplied chain is caller-owned like any explicit list: it keeps its order and carries no `configured` provenance, so `fallbackPriority` never reorders it (`c9d4b46a`). Without a hook list the opt-in and priority behave as before. The second merge conflicted in four files with independent main changes and keeps both sides: async credential preparation in the command attempt and its auth selection (#169111, #169449), the narrower explicit-`thinkingLevel` check in `sessions.patch` (#169435), and simplified model-override bookkeeping (#169458). The generated config baseline was regenerated with `pnpm config:docs:gen`, not merged by hand; over main it adds only this PR's four `fallbackPriority` paths.
- Current `main` (`50520de18`) is merged again (merge commit `a3ea3364`, no rebase; 6402 main commits). 19 files conflicted, all with independent main refactors: #175837 replaced the follow-up admission module with `reply-agent-turn-preparation` (this PR's one-line policy capture at the fence moved there with its test) and split the cron prompt executor into `run-prompt-executor` (the cron fallback options moved there); main renamed the command attempt parameter type to `AgentAttemptParams`, renamed compaction's seed flag, replaced the auto-revert's `assertCurrent` with an expected-session check, and flattened several test files. The generated config baseline was regenerated with `pnpm config:docs:gen` (core 2570 -> 2574, this PR's four paths). `cefea027` keeps the line caps main is already at: the fallback-policy RPC test moved to `server.sessions.store-rpc.fallback-policy.test.ts`, the live-switch ownership check is one helper in `model-fallback-attempt.ts`, and the command attempt reads the stored policy once. `fa3ac2ef` follows main's session-controller mailbox in the queue refresh tests (queued work is submitted, not pushed) and prepares the runtime config snapshot the logical-turn entry now requires (hosted CI found the same need in the hook fallback-priority test; fixed in the following commit).
- On head `8f408dd7`: 11 selection, queue, admission and retry files passed 298 tests; all 45 cron isolated-agent files passed 499, `live-model-switch` 24 and the two attempt-recovery files 117; 15 feature files, including the hook-chain test and main's hook tests, passed 289; 35 files from main that use these symbols or cover the merged areas passed 840. Formatting, focused syntax lint, line-cap, assertion, mock-export and timeout-race guards, `git diff --check`, `config:docs:check` and `protocol:check` passed against current main; the typecheck and the database-worker ratchet have no local result (see the validation limits).
- On head `a07d1d8b`: 37 selection, queue, admission, retry, live-switch, attempt-recovery, logical-turn entry, command attempt, cron policy, session patch and picker files, including the new RPC sibling test, passed 985 tests across 8 Vitest shards (unit-fast 20, gateway 195, infra 321, cron 32, auto-reply 75, agents-core 119, agents-embedded-agent-run 136, agents-support 87; one bounded local unit, one worker); the 7 remaining PR test files (compaction and hook fallback priority, live-switch worker, priority resolver, session entry selection and projection contract, cron payload fallbacks) passed 56 tests across 6 shards. RED on the merged tree with only the production part of `d6ee8ef5` reverted: `agent-runner-execution-state` 2 failed / 8 passed (the withdrawal on a turn admitted on the default, and the return of an opted-in pin to the default). Type-aware `oxlint` on the 75 changed TypeScript files: 0 errors. `run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json`: 0 type errors (peak 2.2 GB in a bounded unit). Line-cap ratchet against main `50520de18`: no new violations or over-cap growth. An independent review of the full diff at P1 scope found no accepted findings (Claude engine; Codex was unavailable here with 401).

| Review finding | Fix | Regression tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `878d39db` P1: a queued follow-up keeps `configured` after a strict `/model` switch | `b6b787ab`: directive, picker, `sessions.patch` and fallback-accounting refreshes publish the committed policy; a queued route rewrite without a policy withdraws it; thinking-only edits and session rotation keep it | `queue/state`, `directive-handling.mixed-inline`, `apply-session-model-selection`, `sessions-patch.preference`, `agent-runner-result-accounting` (real queue) |
| `878d39db` P2: admission refreshes model and source but not the policy | `b6b787ab`: the existing selection capture at the admission fence copies `modelFallbackPolicy` | `followup-turn-admission` |
| `878d39db` P1: a live model-switch retry keeps the old policy | `b6b787ab`: `LiveSessionModelSwitchError` carries the policy; reply and command retries apply it with the route; attempt recovery compares it; compare-before-clear includes it, so a stale completion cannot erase a newer edit | `agent-runner-execution-state`, `agent-command.live-model-switch`, `live-model-switch`, `live-model-switch.worker`, `attempt-recovery`, `model-overrides` |
