## Gaps

- `STATE_DATABASE_READ_ADMISSION_INVALIDATED` is not reproduced and not fixed here. On this base the harness's close no longer overlapped an export on either side, so this run does not exercise a close during an export; no read was refused as invalidated on either side (`invalidated=0`). The seal lifecycle is #162085 territory and is untouched.
- Shared-state WAL checkpoint starvation and shared-state write stalls (#161439, #163748) are a different database and are not addressed.
- Decompression stays inside each slice's transaction (the same SQL decode function as before), so only parsing and projection leave it. Readers are still open for most of a back-to-back export, which is why the `TRUNCATE` probe improves much less than passive checkpoint completion.
- The batch transaction still reads the export statistics over the whole session (`readTranscriptStatsBatchFromDatabase`, which walks every row) for every transcript it reads the head of, including the ones it leaves to the sliced read. The after side logged one `slow SQLite transaction hold` line for the batch transaction in the pair run (1155 ms, before the round 0 line, so the first export) and one in the worker-memory run (1075 ms); the PASSIVE arms logged none.
- Transcripts above the 4 MiB retention limit are no longer read from the batch's SQLite snapshot: each is read after the batch transaction from its own, later snapshot (internally consistent through the version check). Transcripts within the limit, the only ones the cache retains, still share the batch snapshot as on main. Main's batch already returned each transcript as its own entry, and #170404 states that later transcript notifications catch writes after the pass snapshot; I found no consumer that compares entries of one batch with each other, but I did not audit every caller of `buildSessionEntries`.
- Transcripts within the 4 MiB limit are still decoded, parsed and projected inside the batch transaction, as on main, for a group of up to eight sources (the group bound #170404 records); this change does not shorten that hold and I did not measure it.
- The slices are tied together by the transcript context version (rewrite generation, highest raw seq, `transcript_updated_at`), not by one SQLite snapshot, and the same token also decides whether the batch's head is reused. A writer that changed stored rows below the fence without changing any of those three could let one read combine rows from two states, or reuse a head that no longer describes them. Every rewrite path I read changes one of them (`rotateTranscriptGenerationInTransaction` or `touchTranscriptMutationInTransaction` in the transcript store and suffix paths), and `SessionManager` writes already rely on the same token; payload re-encoding (`createTranscriptPayloadUpdater`) changes the stored form, not the decoded event. I did not audit every writer.
- Any append to the same session between two slices changes the raw seq, so that read falls back to the whole-transcript read in one transaction, with the base path's hold. How often that happens for an actively written session under real traffic is not measured; the harness writer appends to a different session.
- The 2 MiB budget is a fixed constant. A slice holds at most 2 MiB of payload text plus the one row that crosses the budget (a compressed row decodes to at most 4 MiB by the table's `CHECK`; a plain `event_json` row has no size check). A large transcript takes about 300 short transactions per export on this fixture instead of one.
- Warm exports of the large session through the memory batch are slower after the change: 2.7%, 2.5% and 1.5% in the three memory sets; in the pair, 3.3% slower (rounds 1 to 3, 1170.3 against 1133.3 ms) and 3.1% slower over the exports of the 20 s probe (1204 against 1168 ms); in the worker-memory run, 1.1% slower (1176.3 against 1163.3 ms). The sliced side runs about 300 short transactions per export, each with a read-only borrow and a context-version read; I did not profile which part costs the difference.
- With exports running, the writer's p99 append latency is higher after the change in all three PASSIVE repetitions (9.7 to 11.1 ms against 5.7 to 7.0 ms), and its mean append count is 5.8% lower (see Evidence). I did not profile this either.
- Under the TRUNCATE probe the writer completed 24% fewer appends after the change (567 against 743) while 2.7 times as many TRUNCATE checkpoints completed; not measured separately.
- PostgreSQL is not sliced: large transcripts are read in one snapshot as on main. The PostgreSQL proof is a statement-level test, not a load run with concurrent writers.
- The cap was enforced by a footprint supervisor on macOS, not by a Linux cgroup, so page-cache accounting and reclaim under a cgroup are not exercised. The test host has 512 GiB, so only the process was capped, not the host.

<details>
<summary>Further gaps</summary>

- Per-sync work is still proportional to the whole transcript for large sessions: the memory session entry keeps an incremental projection only for transcripts up to 4 MiB (`MAX_SNAPSHOT_BYTES` in `session-memory-entry.worker.ts`), so this fixture's session is decoded whole on every export, and one session-entry worker serializes behind it.
- The fenced reader (`loadTranscriptReadSnapshotSync`, used by hydration, `SessionManager` open and reload, the incognito history worker, the bundled session-memory hook capture, `loadTranscriptEventsSync` and `prepareTranscriptCommit`) still decodes and parses a whole transcript inside one read transaction, as on main. #171467 is about the memory session index, its hold was never measured, and `prepareTranscriptCommit` calls it inside an outer transaction where slicing releases nothing; it belongs in a follow-up with its own measurement.
- Readers that decode inside a writer or other outer transaction (`loadTranscriptEventsFromDatabase` callers in message cut, parent session, recovery, transcript mirror and incognito lifecycle; `prepareTranscriptCommit`) and `inspectTranscriptEventsSync` (Doctor one-shot) keep their in-transaction decode. Their writers need the decode and the rows to share one authoritative snapshot, and moving it is a write-path change that this PR does not need.
- The checkpoint probes use their own connection with `busy_timeout = 0` (`TRUNCATE`) or every 250 ms (`PASSIVE`); they measure whether a reader snapshot is open, not how the production checkpoint owner schedules work.
- The fixture is synthetic (random-word text, one large session). Compression ratio and decode cost on real transcripts differ; absolute milliseconds and MiB will differ on other hosts.
- #160386 also proposes delta ingestion in Memory Core (index only the events after the last indexed seq). This PR does not do that and does not reduce the total decode work of an export; it only bounds how long a read snapshot is held.

</details>

prs.title: perf(memory): evict superseded embedding cache rows first at the cap
prs.body:
Refs #114612

## What Problem This Solves

`memory_embedding_cache` is capped at 50,000 rows. When new vectors would take it past the cap (the insertion reservation, `reserveMemoryEmbeddingCacheCapacity`) or it is already over the cap (the post-publication `cache.prune`), the cache deletes the rows with the oldest `updated_at`. It does not look at whether a published chunk still uses a row.

Editing a memory file changes its chunk hashes, so the vectors for the old text are never read again, but they keep their place in the cap. A cache that sits at the cap is mostly such rows, and plain oldest-first order deletes a vector that a live, unchanged chunk still needs whenever that vector is older than the superseded ones. The next full reindex then pays the provider to embed unchanged text again. This happens on both storage engines: the SQLite agent database and the PostgreSQL memory store.

## User Impact

At the cap, the vectors of unchanged indexed text survive eviction while superseded vectors are available to take their place, so a forced reindex of unchanged content makes no provider request. In the real CLI runs below, on a store seeded to the 50,000-row cap with superseded vectors and three new files added, the base build deleted the vector of an unchanged file and re-embedded it on the next reindex (1 request); the head build made 0 requests. The result is the same on SQLite and on PostgreSQL (`database.engine: "postgres"`).

Nothing changes below the cap, and the number of rows deleted at the cap is the same as before. The schema, config, and row cap do not change.

## Why This Change Was Made

`docs/concepts/memory-builtin.md` describes the cache as bounded by the existing row cap. The bound stays exactly as it is; this change only decides which rows fill the deletions the cap already makes.

The change keeps the shape the current owners of this code gave it, and adds the preference inside it:

- #174183 (`feat(memory): index and publish memory on PostgreSQL`): "PostgreSQL eviction uses the canonical composite cache key; SQLite keeps its existing statements." The preference is added inside the same `deleteOldestMemoryEmbeddingCacheRows` helper, before its engine split. PostgreSQL still deletes by the `(provider, model, provider_key, hash)` tuple ordered by `updated_at` and then that key; SQLite still deletes by `rowid` ordered by `updated_at, rowid`, so #175224's "Replacements preserve row identity, which remains the tie-breaker for equal-timestamp eviction" holds in both passes.
- #170792 ("The publication worker retains the cache size and updates it only after committed inserts/deletes") and #175224, which kept that retained size: `pruneMemoryEmbeddingCache` and `reserveMemoryEmbeddingCacheCapacity` keep their signatures' meaning and return the retained size computed from the rows actually deleted. Both publication workers keep their `writeCache((size) => ...)` wrapping.
- #175566 ("Only when a write could exceed the cap does it count the real size, delete the rows being replaced, and evict the oldest excess before inserting"): the reservation keeps that sequence and the excess it computes. Only the choice of which rows make up that excess changes. #175566 notes that its own change leaves eviction order alone ("eviction order only changes among rows written in the same millisecond"); this change alters that order on purpose, which is the retention point below.

The eviction preference is narrow on purpose:

- Only rows of the active provider identities are preferred. Rows of any other provider, model, or provider key keep plain oldest-first order, so a fallback or previously configured provider is not singled out.
- A preferred row has no published chunk carrying its hash, and was written before the oldest published chunk. A full reindex rewrites every chunk, so after one such a row predates the index that dropped it.
- A row written at or after the oldest published chunk keeps plain oldest-first order even when nothing references it yet. It may be a vector a failed rebuild cached for its retry, or one another sync cached and has not published.
- The fence is read from `memory_index_chunks` in SQL on both engines, so it holds across processes and restarts. No new state is kept in memory.
- The deletion count is computed exactly as before. Preferred rows fill it first; if there are fewer, the remainder is taken oldest-first, as today. At or below the cap nothing is deleted.

The review checkpoint in `docs/reference/database-schemas/storage-changes.md` says "Changing which valid data is retained or deleted still needs acceptance." This change does that: when the cap deletes, it picks superseded vectors of the active identities before other rows. #114612 is the linked discussion for cache retention. The points that checkpoint asks for:

- Store and lifecycle: `memory_embedding_cache` in the agent store (SQLite agent database or the PostgreSQL agent schema), written only by the publication workers inside their existing write transactions.
- Source versus derived: derived. Any deleted vector can be recomputed by the provider; #170792 calls it "this disposable cache".
- New persistence: none. The fence and the reference check are read from `memory_index_chunks` in the same statement.
- Retention and deletion: the cap and the number of rows deleted are unchanged; only the order changes. `memory-builtin.md` documented the old order ("removes the oldest entries"), and that sentence is updated.
- Schema, upgrade, downgrade: unchanged on both engines; the runs below show the head build on a base-written store and a base build reading a head-written store with no provider request.
- Concurrency and recovery: the fence holds across processes and restarts because it is SQL; a failed rebuild deletes nothing extra (CLI step C on each engine).

## The change in one sentence

Capacity eviction of `memory_embedding_cache`, on SQLite and PostgreSQL, first takes, oldest first, active-identity rows that no published chunk references and that were written before the oldest published chunk, then falls back to plain oldest-first for the rest of the same, unchanged count.

Diff shape against `main`: 11 files, 641 insertions and 49 deletions. Production is 119 insertions and 44 deletions in 6 files, docs 12 and 3, tests 510 and 2 in 4 files.

- `manager-embedding-cache.ts` (+87/-34): `deleteOldestMemoryEmbeddingCacheRows` gains an optional `unreferencedFirst` argument. Its existing per-engine query becomes a local `deleteOldest(count, identities)` that applies the preference filter when identities are given; the helper runs it once with the preference and once without for the remainder. `pruneMemoryEmbeddingCache`, `upsertMemoryEmbeddingCache`, and `reserveMemoryEmbeddingCacheCapacity` pass the argument through.
- `cache.prune` input and the cache upsert header carry `unreferencedFirst: { identities }` (`manager-publication-task.ts`). The SQLite worker (`manager-publication.worker.ts`) and the PostgreSQL publication handler (`manager-publication-postgres.ts`) forward it to `pruneMemoryEmbeddingCache`; the insertion path already passes the header through. `manager-embedding-cache-ops.ts` fills it from the sync's provider identities.
- `manager-database-context.ts`: `pruneEmbeddingCache` takes the `cache.prune` input instead of a bare `maxEntries`. The signature is written on one line through a local `CachePruneInput` alias, and the return expression is a `const` followed by `return pruned ?? false`, so the file stays at 700 counted lines, the cap the line-cap ratchet enforces.
- Docs: `docs/concepts/memory-builtin.md`.

The identity comparison casts the TEXT key columns on SQLite only (`CAST(provider AS text)` and so on). This is a no-op on values. It stops SQLite from answering the identity filter through the primary key and then sorting every matching row by `updated_at`, which reads each vector. With it, SQLite walks the `updated_at` index and stops at the limit. In the benchmark below, removing only the cast makes the median batch cost 120.025 ms with 1,000 chunks and 105.491 ms with 10,000 chunks, against 1.517 ms and 7.714 ms with it. PostgreSQL compares the plain columns.

## Contract

| Case | Engine | Outcome | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cache at or below the cap | both | nothing deleted | unchanged |
| Insertion or prune past the cap | both | same number of rows deleted as before | unchanged cap and retained size |
| Active-identity row, no published chunk carries its hash, written before the oldest published chunk | both | deleted first, oldest first (SQLite ties by `rowid`, PostgreSQL by the canonical key) | superseded text |
| Row a published chunk carries | both | deleted only when no preferred row is left, oldest first | live content |
| Active-identity unreferenced row written at or after the oldest published chunk | both | plain oldest-first | a retry's or another sync's unpublished vector |
| Rows of another provider, model, or provider key | both | plain oldest-first | a fallback or previous provider may be switched back to |
| Empty published index, or no active identities | both | plain oldest-first | no fence |
| Full rebuild fails before publication | both | no extra deletion; the retry reuses cached vectors | unchanged failure semantics; CLI step C on each engine |
| Incremental sync | both | same rule; unchanged chunks keep their `updated_at`, so the fence is older and fewer rows qualify | the fence never moves past a live chunk |
| Schema, config keys, public API | both | unchanged | none added |

## Upgrade and rollback compatibility

No `.sql` file, migration, table, column, or index changes on either engine, and the SQLite agent `PRAGMA user_version` is 31 before and after (transcript below). The only persisted effect is which rows remain after a deletion the cap already makes.

- Upgrade: on both engines the head build runs `memory index --force` on a store the base build created and filled to the cap, exit 0. The vector of the unchanged `delta.md` keeps its row and its original `updated_at`, and rows of another identity are untouched.
- Rollback (SQLite): the base build runs `memory index --force` on the store the head build last wrote, with 0 provider requests and no change to live-row or chunk checksums, then answers `memory search`.

## Gaps, stated plainly

- **Which rows survive at the cap changes.** The count, cap, schema, and rollback do not change, but the documented order ("removes the oldest entries") does, on both engines. Under the storage review checkpoint that is a retention change that needs acceptance. A superseded vector can be deleted before a live one that is newer. If its text is restored later, that costs one re-embedding, and under plain oldest-first the same row would usually have gone anyway, because it is old.
- **The fence is the oldest published chunk across all sources and models.** After incremental syncs it can be far in the past, so fewer rows qualify, and the eviction falls back to oldest-first. Nothing extra is deleted.
- **The fence compares clocks.** Chunk and cache `updated_at` both come from `Date.now()` in the writing process. A writer whose clock runs behind can make a row look older than it is, and a vector another sync cached before the oldest chunk of a newly published index, and has not published yet, counts as superseded. The only effect is on order (at worst one re-embedding). The count is unchanged.
- **Eviction is slower when there are many chunks.** `memory_index_chunks` has no index on `hash` or `updated_at`, so both subqueries scan it. A 100-row batch takes about 8 ms on SQLite and 5.6 ms on PostgreSQL with 10,000 chunks, and about 29 ms and 13 ms with 40,000, against under 1 ms and about 2 to 3.4 ms oldest-first. When no row qualifies (scenario W) the cost is paid without a benefit. It runs only above the cap; larger indexes were not measured.
- **PostgreSQL has no manager-level test.** The caller wiring in `manager-embedding-cache-ops.ts` is shared by both engines; on SQLite the manager cases fail when it drops the preference, on PostgreSQL only the CLI run exercises it (the PostgreSQL unit and publication files stay green under those two mutations). The PostgreSQL handler's forwarding is pinned by `manager-publication.postgres.test.ts`.
- **Not pinned by a test:** the `model` part of the identity comparison (the unit identities differ by provider and provider key), the equal-timestamp tie-break inside the preferred pass, and the SQLite cast (covered by the benchmark only).
- **Stale identities, byte budgets, and age-based retention are not addressed.** Rows of a provider the user switched away from keep plain oldest-first order. The row cap is still the only bound.
- **Real-provider proof was not run.** The CLI runs use a local stub provider. No built Gateway process was run; the CLI uses the same manager and publication workers.
- **Rollback was run on SQLite only.** The PostgreSQL arms prove the upgrade path (base-written store, head build) but not a base build on a head-written PostgreSQL store.
- **Full suite not run.** `pnpm changed:lanes --json` for this diff reports `extensions`, `extensionTests`, and `docs` true and every other lane false; the owning directory and the PostgreSQL conformance selection are the suites this diff can break. CI covers the rest.

auto_merge.commit_title: perf(memory): evict superseded embedding cache rows first at the cap (#164792)
auto_merge.commit_message:
* perf(memory): evict superseded embedding cache rows first at the cap

- Capacity eviction (insertion-time reservation and the post-publication
  prune) removes the same number of rows as before, but first takes rows of
  the active provider identities that no published chunk references and that
  were written before the oldest published chunk, oldest first.
- Newer unreferenced rows (a retry's or another sync's unpublished vectors)
  and other identities keep plain oldest-first order. Nothing is removed at
  or below the cap.
- cache.prune carries the preference to the publication worker; the
  insertion header carries it for staged upserts. No schema change.
- Identity columns are compared through CAST so SQLite walks the updated_at
  index to the limit instead of sorting every row through the primary key.
- Docs describe the eviction order.

* simplify: drop duplicate cache eviction tests

- Remove manager cases for within-cap pruning and for rebuilds that fail
  before publication or partway through a source; the unit prune case and
  manager.reindex-recovery.test.ts already own those paths, and the partway
  case sat at the cap so no eviction policy could fail it.
- Drop the second rebuild and the full-row echo from the full-rebuild case;
  the hash list already proves the live rows survive.
- Drop the plain oldest-first arm of the insertion reservation case and the
  single-identity runs of the fallback case, which repeat existing coverage.
- Production files are unchanged.

* perf(memory): evict superseded embedding cache rows first at the cap

- Capacity eviction in manager-embedding-cache.ts first takes, oldest first,
  active-identity rows that no published chunk references and that were written
  before the oldest published chunk, then plain oldest-first for the rest of the
  unchanged count.
- The preference lives in the owner's deleteOldestMemoryEmbeddingCacheRows and its
  existing SQLite (rowid) and PostgreSQL (canonical key tuple) branches, reached by
  reserveMemoryEmbeddingCacheCapacity and pruneMemoryEmbeddingCache, which keep
  returning the retained cache size.
- The cache upsert header and the cache.prune input carry unreferencedFirst to both
  publication backends; no config, schema, or threshold is added.
- Tests: SQLite and PostgreSQL cache cases and four manager cases.

* simplify: drop within-cap eviction assertions that only exercise main's early return

- pruneMemoryEmbeddingCache returns before the preference is consulted at or below the cap; that branch is unchanged from main
- removes the re-seed and assertion from the SQLite and PostgreSQL unit cases

* style(memory): keep the cache prune signature within the context line cap

- one-line pruneEmbeddingCache signature via a local CachePruneInput alias
- manager-database-context.ts stays at 700 counted lines, as on main

prs.title: fix(web-push): agent-finished pushes were indistinguishable across sessions
prs.body:
Closes #143946

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: agent-finished Web Push notifications are indistinguishable when more than one session runs under the same agent — every notification renders the generic "An agent completed its response."

## User Impact

User impact: agent-finished pushes now identify themselves with the conversation's actual reply (e.g. "Deploy finished, tests green."), prefixed with the agent name when the payload identifies it. Users who prefer not to see content keep the generic body — the existing detail-level and per-category notification preferences govern this unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

#143946 noted `agent-finished` is the only remaining event-push category without a producer-owned label. This follows the same `identifiedBody` pattern `scheduled-task-failed` and `human-mentioned` already use: the first readable text of the final assistant message, whitespace-normalized, capped at 140 chars with an ellipsis, falling back to the generic body when the message carries nothing readable. Privacy posture is unchanged — `identifiedBody` is consumed only for non-private detail levels by the existing delivery gate, so `private` recipients keep the generic body and no icon.

## Evidence

- `src/gateway/event-web-push.test.ts`: 43/43 passing (39 pre-existing + 4 new):
  - final assistant text lands as the identified body
  - agent label prefix when the payload identifies the agent
  - long replies truncate to ≤140 chars with an ellipsis
  - whitespace-only text keeps the generic body
- Targeted run: `vitest run src/gateway/event-web-push.test.ts` → 43 passed.
- `pnpm check` on this branch: all sub-checks pass except the pre-existing `max-lines suppression ratchet` failure, which reproduces identically on pristine `main` (three `ui/src/pages/**` files, untouched by this PR).

prs.title: improve(memory): faster repeated memory keyword searches
prs.body:
Related: #114777, #149793

## What Problem This Solves

Repeated memory keyword searches recompile their SQL on every search, so the statement cache added in #114777 saves nothing for them.

Keyword search runs four statements per request on the memory search worker's retained read-only connection, which has the bounded statement cache enabled. Two things make SQLite recompile them on every run:

- Each search calls `db.function(...)` again for `openclaw_memory_normalized_contains` and `openclaw_memory_exact_path_specificity` (3 calls per search on these stores). Replacing an existing SQL function expires every prepared statement on the connection, including FTS5's own cached statements.
- The statements bind a bare `LIMIT ?` (all four) and `LIKE ? ESCAPE '\'` (the exact-path statement). Since SQLite 3.47, a bare bound LIMIT value or LIKE pattern is marked as plan-relevant (`select.c:2538` and `whereexpr.c:208-215` in 3.53.4), and `node:sqlite` clears bindings before every run, so a cached handle with such a parameter is recompiled on each run.

Through a real `gateway run`, 30 `memory.search` requests on base registered the two functions 90 times and recompiled the four search statements on every request, although the cache had stopped calling `prepare` after the second request.

## User Impact

User impact: memory keyword searches, including the keyword half of hybrid searches (both run the same worker query), spend less CPU per request on the memory search worker; results are identical.

| Measure | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `db.function` calls, 30 Gateway `memory.search` requests | 90 (3 per request) | 2 (first request only) |
| Search statement recompiles, Gateway requests 3 to 30 | 4 per request | 0 |
| SQLite authorizer callbacks per Gateway request (3 to 30) | 147 | 5 |
| Time per search, real store with 6,012 chunks (quiet host) | 1173.3 us | 1001.9 us (171.4 us, 14.6 percent less) |
| Time per search, real store with 43,634 chunks (quiet host) | 3656.7 us | 3515.6 us (141.2 us, 3.9 percent less) |

The saving is a fixed amount of compile work per search, so its share shrinks as query execution grows with the index. It is CPU on the worker thread; the Gateway's own millisecond-resolution `memory.search` latency (about 22 to 24 ms per request in these runs) cannot resolve it. Nothing an operator configures or stores changes, and no config key, schema, migration or stored byte changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The statement cache (#114777, raised to 64 entries in #149793) exists so hot synchronous statements are compiled once and reused. Memory keyword search is one of the hottest read paths on the agent database, and both causes above defeat that cache for it. Either cause alone keeps the four statements recompiling on every search, so this change removes both; builds with only one half are measured in Evidence.

## The change in one sentence

Register the two memory search SQL functions once per connection and let each search swap the state they read, and bind the search LIMIT values and LIKE patterns as `LIMIT +?` and `LIKE (? || '')` so SQLite no longer treats them as plan inputs.

Diff: 3 files, 132 insertions, 20 deletions. Production: `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.ts` (+43/-16, including 9 new comment lines). Tests: `manager-search.test.ts` (+84, one new `describe`) and `manager-search-worker.sqlite.test.ts` (+5/-4, the four pinned keyword statement hashes and one comment line, see Tests).

- Registration: a module-level `WeakMap<DatabaseSync, state>` holds the substring matchers and the exact-path matcher. The first search on a connection registers both functions with the same names, argument counts, `deterministic: true` flag and return values; later searches assign the state. This follows the per-connection memo `loadedExtensions` in `manager-publication.worker.ts` in the same directory. `searchKeyword` and `searchPathKeyword` run their statements synchronously after setting the state, so no other search can interleave on the connection.
- SQL: `LIMIT ?` becomes `LIMIT +?` in the four search statements and `LIKE ? ESCAPE '\'` becomes `LIKE (? || '') ESCAPE '\'` in the exact-path statement. A unary plus or a concatenation is not a bare variable, so SQLite does not mark it; the bound values and results are the same. A comment at the top of the module cites the SQLite source lines so a later cleanup does not revert it.

| Input case | Expected outcome |
|---|---|
| Body search with substring terms (trigram, non-ASCII) | Same rows, scores and order; matchers set before the statement runs |
| Path search, exact and lexical partitions | Same rows; exact-path specificity read from the current query's matcher |
| Searches with different queries on one connection, sequential or interleaved at their `await` points | Each statement uses its own search's matchers (the test compares every sequential and repeated result with a fresh connection, and the interleaved results with the sequential ones) |
| `matchAny` retry and MATCH failure fallback | Unchanged; they set the state through the same call before running |
| First search on a new connection | Registers both functions once (2 calls), as before it registered them on first use |
| Connection closed and reopened as a new `DatabaseSync` | New object, new registration |
| PostgreSQL | Not on this path (`searchPostgresMemoryKeyword`) |
| Query plans | Identical for every executed statement shape (below) |

Unchanged: function names, arity, `deterministic`, return values, statement count and order per search, the statement cache policy (capacity, second-use admission), schema, config, stored data, the vector and KNN statements, and the dialect construct counts (`SQLite dialect design (changed files): 1 -> 1.`).

## Evidence

All of the following ran on one machine (Mac Studio Mac15,14, macOS 27.0.1 arm64, Node v24.21.0, SQLite 3.53.4 from `node:sqlite`) against base `a7e31844f2e` and this branch. The measured AFTER build was made from an earlier commit of this branch whose production code differs from the final commit only in comments; the final commit rebuilt is byte-identical in every built JavaScript chunk; only files that embed the commit and build time differ (`gates-final/tree-identity.out`, `gates-final/dist-rebuild-diff.out`). Scripts and raw outputs: https://github.com/etzelm/openclaw/tree/e9a04b920c5a4711a40c0e7d416044a7eb4702a1

### Build

`pnpm build` succeeded for both arms (`build/`):

```
[build-all] phase timings: total 4m 15.5s; slowest write-unified-entry-dts 2m 7.6s; tsdown-packages 26.9s; tsdown 26.3s; ui:build 14.6s; runtime-postbuild 13.9s; check-cli-bootstrap-imports 9.81s; external-plugins:local-dist 9.65s; tsdown-ai 6.89s; write-cli-startup-metadata 5.61s; plugins:assets:build 5.23s; plugins:assets:copy 4.45s; check-plugin-sdk-exports 1.30s; build-stamp 263ms; write-build-info 142ms; runtime-postbuild-stamp 85ms; native-protocol 79ms
[build-all] phase timings: total 4m 14.5s; slowest write-unified-entry-dts 2m 7.8s; tsdown-packages 26.9s; tsdown 26.3s; ui:build 14.5s; runtime-postbuild 13.6s; check-cli-bootstrap-imports 9.95s; external-plugins:local-dist 8.95s; tsdown-ai 6.86s; write-cli-startup-metadata 5.49s; plugins:assets:build 5.22s; plugins:assets:copy 4.29s; check-plugin-sdk-exports 1.50s; build-stamp 313ms; write-build-info 118ms; runtime-postbuild-stamp 87ms; native-protocol 80ms
```

The first line is BEFORE, the second AFTER. In the built search chunk the only differences are the registration code and the SQL text (`prod/dist-diff.out`):

```
-      ORDER BY rank ${rankOrder} LIMIT ?`;
+      ORDER BY rank ${rankOrder} LIMIT +?`;
...
-	params.db.function(EXACT_PATH_SPECIFICITY_SQL_FUNCTION, { deterministic: true }, (candidatePath) => typeof candidatePath === "string" ? matchExactPath(candidatePath) : 0);
+	db.function(EXACT_PATH_SPECIFICITY_SQL_FUNCTION, { deterministic: true }, (candidatePath) => typeof candidatePath === "string" ? state.matchExactPath(candidatePath) : 0);
```

### Behavior through the shipped Gateway and CLI

Both builds ran through their shipped entry point, `node openclaw.mjs`, with their own `HOME` and `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, a clean environment and `memory.search.provider: "none"` (keyword only, no network). A seeded generator wrote the same synthetic workspace in both arms (manifest sha256 equal), and `memory index --force --agent main --verbose` built a store of 401 files and 3,626 chunks in each (`proof/`).

The code logs nothing about statement compilation, so a read-only preload loaded with `NODE_OPTIONS=--import=...` (`proof/tools/observe-search-prepare.mjs`) wraps `DatabaseSync.prototype.prepare`, `function` and the statement run methods, and installs a counting authorizer through the prototype `setAuthorizer` before the first search statement (the instance wrapper would disable the statement cache). An authorizer callback fires only while SQLite compiles a statement, so callbacks that read `memory_index_chunks` during a run are a recompile. It changes no OpenClaw source; timing runs used a variant without the authorizer.

`gateway run --port <port> --bind loopback --auth token --token <test-token> --allow-unconfigured`, then 30 `gateway call memory.search` requests cycling five queries, observed in the Gateway process and its worker threads (`proof/summary.md`, `proof/gateway/<arm>/c1/`):

| Arm | `db.function` calls | Search statement `prepare` calls, requests 1 / 2 / 3 to 30 | Recompiles, requests 1 / 2 / 3 to 30 | Authorizer callbacks per request, 3 to 30 | Total callbacks, 30 requests |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | 3 per request, 90 total | 4 / 4 / 0 | 8 / 8 / 4 each | 147 | 4644 |
| patched | 2 on request 1, 2 total | 4 / 4 / 0 | 4 / 4 / 0 | 5 | 409 |

Both arms prepare the statements on the first two requests (the cache admits a statement on its second use) and never again. On base the cached handles still recompile on every request; on this branch they do not. The 5 callbacks left per request are FTS5's own sorter statement, which FTS5 prepares for every `ORDER BY rank` query: a parameterless FTS5 control query shows the same `SELECT 1, FUNCTION 1, READ 3` callbacks on every run, and none without `ORDER BY rank` (`fts5/fts5-sorter-control.out`).

Summed search statement time per request, timing observer without the authorizer, median of requests 11 to 30, runs in the order base, patched, patched, base with a Gateway restart each (`proof/summary.md`, section D): base 4047.6 and 4085.7 us, patched 3922.1 and 3772.8 us. The host was busy during these runs (1-minute load average 21.40 to 30.85), so the production-path timings below are the better measure of size.

`memory search "<query>" --json --agent main --max-results 25` from the CLI, five queries, each a new process: exit 0 and 25 results in every run. A one-shot process runs each statement once, so reuse across searches cannot show there, but the recompile on first run still does: per process, base 3 `db.function` calls, 8 compiles and 270 authorizer callbacks; patched 2, 4 and 153.

Search results are identical between arms for all five queries, through the CLI and all six Gateway runs (sha256 of `[path, startLine, endLine, score]` in result order, `proof/parity.md`), and `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` is identical for every statement shape (`proof/plans.md`).

### Behavior through the production search function on real stores

The built `searchKeywordWithFallback` of each arm was called as `executeMemorySearchWorkerQuery` calls it, with the request the manager builds by default (`limit` 24, `exactPathLimit` 200, `snippetMaxChars` 700, source `memory`, `unicode61`, `boostFallbackRanking`; derivation with file and line in `prod/params.md`). The stores are two private agent databases taken with `openclaw backup sqlite create`; the agent read-only opener refuses these schema 24 snapshots, so both arms opened them with the built `openSqliteReadOnlyDatabase` (the layer that opener uses) and the built `enableNodeSqliteKyselyStatementCache`, as the retained reader does. The inputs are 8 common words and 12 file-name stems drawn from each store; only counts, hashes, timings and plans are published.

Per search, first 10 searches on one connection, counting authorizer installed before the first search (`prod/compiles-dev.out`, `prod/compiles-main.out`, the same on both stores):

```
reads of memory_index_chunks while compiling   BEFORE 86 86 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43   AFTER 43 43 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
db.function calls                              BEFORE  3  3  3  3  3  3  3  3  3  3   AFTER  2  0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
```

Over a later 60-search run on each store, base had 2,580 such reads and 180 `db.function` calls; this branch had 0 and 0.

Warm timing in one process: 2 warm-up passes over the 20 inputs, then 5 reps of N searches each (400 on the 6,012-chunk store, 200 on the 43,634-chunk store), mean per search per rep, fresh process per run. Two interleaved rounds (base, patched, patched, base) ran at 1-minute load averages of 7.2 to 10.7; 8 more runs in the order base, patched, patched, base, base, patched, patched, base ran at 3.4 to 3.6 (`prod/timing-dev.out`, `prod/timing-main.out`, raw rep means included):

| Store | Runs | Base, median us per search | Patched | Saving |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6,012 chunks | rounds 1 / 2 | 1198.4 / 1311.6 | 1126.0 / 1096.2 | 6.0 / 16.4 percent |
| 6,012 chunks | 8 quiet runs, 20 rep means per arm | 1173.3 | 1001.9 | 171.4 us, 14.6 percent |
| 43,634 chunks | rounds 1 / 2 | 4068.1 / 3872.1 | 3553.7 / 3702.0 | 12.6 / 4.4 percent |
| 43,634 chunks | 8 quiet runs, 20 rep means per arm | 3656.7 | 3515.6 | 141.2 us, 3.9 percent |

Over both loaded rounds, the medians of all 10 rep means per arm are 1239.9 to 1111.4 us (10.4 percent) and 3950.9 to 3618.8 us (8.4 percent); over all 30 rep means per arm, 14.1 and 4.4 percent. Single loaded rounds swing by more than the effect, so User Impact quotes the quiet runs.

Results: the sha256 of the full result object (`body` and `path` rows with scores and errors) is identical for 20 of 20 inputs on both stores (`prod/parity-dev.out`, `prod/parity-main.out`; 227 body and 49 path rows on the smaller store, 408 and 148 on the larger, no errors).

Plans: every executed statement was explained with its own bound values on the same connection, in both arms. 80 of 80 identical on each store, four statement shapes (`prod/plans-dev.out`, `prod/plans-main.out`). For example the exact-path statement on both arms:

```
MATERIALIZE exact_paths
MATERIALIZE scored_paths
MATERIALIZE pattern_candidates
MATERIALIZE candidates
SCAN memory_index_paths_fts VIRTUAL TABLE INDEX 0:M2
SCAN candidates
SCAN pattern_candidates
SCAN scored_paths
SEARCH live EXISTS USING COVERING INDEX idx_memory_index_chunks_path_source (path=? AND source=?)
USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
SCAN exact_paths
SEARCH c USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_memory_index_chunks_1 (id=?)
CORRELATED SCALAR SUBQUERY 6
SEARCH candidate USING INDEX idx_memory_index_chunks_path_source (path=? AND source=?)
USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
```

The `LIKE` patterns are applied to the path FTS table or to a materialized CTE, neither of which can use an index for `LIKE`, which is why rewriting them does not change a plan.

Either half alone, measured the same way with two more builds of this branch (one with the SQL text reverted to bare `LIMIT ?` and `LIKE ?`, one that registers the functions on every call against the shared state), per steady-state search (search 10) and over a 60-search run on each store (`halves/tables-dev.out`, `halves/tables-main.out`, `halves/compiles-<store>.out`):

| Build | Reads of `memory_index_chunks` while compiling, per search | `db.function` calls per search | FTS5 shadow-table and `PRAGMA data_version` callbacks per search (6,012 / 43,634 chunks) | Total callbacks per search (6,012 / 43,634 chunks) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | 43 | 3 | 26 / 36 | 147 / 160 (147 to 160 by input on the smaller store) |
| registration once, bare `LIMIT ?` and `LIKE ?` | 43 | 0 after the first search | 0 / 0 | 116 / 116 |
| `LIMIT +?` and `LIKE (? || '')`, functions registered on every call | 43 | 6 | 26 / 36 | 147 / 160 (147 to 160 by input on the smaller store) |
| this change | 0 | 0 after the first search | 0 / 0 | 5 / 5 |

Registering once stops the expiry of FTS5's own cached statements (the shadow-table reads) but the bound `LIMIT` and `LIKE` still recompile the four search statements; the rewrite alone is undone by the next registration. Results were identical across all four builds, 20 of 20 inputs on each store (`halves/parity-dev.out`, `halves/parity-main.out`).

Two synthetic stores (3,030 chunks over about 300 paths, including non-ASCII and NFD names) cover what the real stores lack, the `trigram` tokenizer and the pattern-only exact-path statement used for non-ASCII queries: results identical 20 of 20 on each, plans identical on 101 of 101 statements (12 shapes, `unicode61`) and 90 of 90 (18 shapes, `trigram`), the same compile pattern, and 236.2 us (9.6 percent) and 143.8 us (4.1 percent) saved per search (`prod/synthetic-unicode61.out`, `prod/synthetic-trigram.out`).

### Tests

`pnpm test extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search-worker.sqlite.test.ts`:

```
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  12 passed (12)
```

Owning directory, `pnpm test extensions/memory-core/src/memory`:

```
 Test Files  99 passed | 4 skipped (103)
      Tests  911 passed | 23 skipped (934)
```

Consumers outside the directory and the search entry tests, `pnpm test` with `manager-search-orchestration.test.ts`, `manager-search-path.test.ts`, `manager-search-worker.test.ts`, `manager-search.unicode-query.test.ts`, `doctor-contract-api.test.ts`, `memory-forget.test.ts`, `manager-search-worker.sqlite.test.ts` and `manager-search.postgres.test.ts` (the PostgreSQL file skips without a server):

```
 Test Files  7 passed | 1 skipped (8)
      Tests  135 passed | 6 skipped (141)
```

`manager-search-worker.sqlite.test.ts` pins the sha256 of each statement's exact SQL bytes. Its four keyword hashes change because the SQL text changes; the vector fallback and KNN hashes do not. Recomputed from both built trees, each new hash is the sha256 of the base statement with only `LIMIT ?` to `LIMIT +?` and `LIKE ? ESCAPE` to `LIKE (? || '') ESCAPE` applied (`gates-final/baseline-hashes.out`; its fifth line repeats statement 1 because the empty store triggers the relaxed body retry):

```
statement 1: before 4ef955cb... | rewrite(before) 0d8edb57... | after 0d8edb57... | rewrite(before) === after: true | LIMIT ? 1 -> 0, LIKE ? 0 -> 0
statement 2: before e0eb673f... | rewrite(before) d21b7990... | after d21b7990... | rewrite(before) === after: true | LIMIT ? 1 -> 0, LIKE ? 4 -> 0
statement 3: before fa8fb140... | rewrite(before) 0452ff06... | after 0452ff06... | rewrite(before) === after: true | LIMIT ? 1 -> 0, LIKE ? 0 -> 0
statement 4: before 60ff181c... | rewrite(before) 6e57716a... | after 6e57716a... | rewrite(before) === after: true | LIMIT ? 1 -> 0, LIKE ? 0 -> 0
```

### Regression proof (red/green)

The new test (`searchKeywordWithFallback statement reuse`, for `unicode61` and `trigram`) runs three different queries (body terms, an exact file name, a non-ASCII name) on one in-memory connection, first one after another plus a repeat, then all three at once with `Promise.all` (each search awaits between its body and path statements, so they interleave), and spies `db.function` and `db.prepare`. It asserts that each function is registered exactly once, that no search statement contains a bare `LIMIT ?` or `LIKE ?`, that the exact-path and lexical path statements ran, and that the sequential, repeated and interleaved results all equal the same search on a fresh connection. The two guards are soft assertions so a failure reports both causes. The interleaved phase guards later edits: each statement run sets its search's state immediately before it, so neither base nor any build of this change fails that assertion today. A spy cannot see SQLite's internal re-prepare (`node:sqlite` exposes no reprepare counter), so the test guards the two causes rather than the recompile itself; the Evidence above shows the recompile.

On base with only the new test file added (`gates-final/red.out`):

```
 FAIL  |extension-database-workers| extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts > searchKeywordWithFallback statement reuse > keeps unicode61 search statements reusable across searches on one connection
 FAIL  |extension-database-workers| extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts > searchKeywordWithFallback statement reuse > keeps trigram search statements reusable across searches on one connection
AssertionError: expected [ …(25) ] to deeply equal [ …(2) ]
...
 FAIL  |extension-database-workers| extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts > searchKeywordWithFallback statement reuse > keeps unicode61 search statements reusable across searches on one connection
AssertionError: expected [ Array(94) ] to deeply equal []
...
 FAIL  |extension-database-workers| extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts > searchKeywordWithFallback statement reuse > keeps trigram search statements reusable across searches on one connection
AssertionError: expected [ Array(90) ] to deeply equal []
...
 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  2 failed | 7 passed (9)
```

On this branch (`gates-final/green.out`):

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  9 passed (9)
```

Each half is guarded separately. With only the registration change (SQL text reverted), the test fails only on the SQL assertion (`expected [ Array(94) ] to deeply equal []` and `Array(90)`); with only the SQL rewrite (functions registered on every call against the shared state), it fails only on the registration count (`expected [ …(50) ] to deeply equal [ …(2) ]`) (`mutants/mutant-M1.out`, `mutants/mutant-M2.out`).

### Other checks

`pnpm check:changed --base a7e31844f2edcc6a0a783549f1f5c1394ec83fb8`, lanes `extensions, extensionTests`:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| typecheck extensions / extension tests | ok |
| lint extension changed files | ok |
| format changed files | ok |
| SQLite dialect ratchet | ok (`SQLite dialect design (changed files): 1 -> 1.`; `SQLite dialect ratchet OK: no construct-group growth against a7e31844f2edcc6a0a783549f1f5c1394ec83fb8.`) |
| SQLite worker ratchet | ok (`SQLite worker ratchet OK: no T1 call-count growth against a7e31844f2edcc6a0a783549f1f5c1394ec83fb8.`) |
| line-cap growth ratchet | ok (`Line-cap ratchet OK: 3 changed source files; no new violations or over-cap growth.`) |
| mock export, assertion SAFETY, test timeout race ratchets; plugin boundaries; import cycles; database-first legacy-store guard | ok |
| `git diff --check` | clean |
| max-lines suppression ratchet | failed on `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.test.tsx`, `ui/src/pages/config/config-page-state.ts`, `ui/src/pages/sessions/sessions-page-state.ts`; none are in this diff, and the same check fails on the same three files in a clean checkout of `a7e31844f2e` (`gates-final/base-checks.out`) |
| dead export scan | failed on 8 production and 7 full-tree exports (for example `src/agents/model-auth-env-vars.ts: listKnownProviderEnvApiKeyNames`); none are in this diff, and the same scan lists the same 15 exports in a clean checkout of `a7e31844f2e` (`gates-final/base-checks.out`) |

### Measured test cost

`pnpm test extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`, arms interleaved, each tree warmed once first (`gates-final/cost/`):

| Run | Arm | 1-minute load before | Wall | Shard | Tests | New cases |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | base | 47.03 | 18.54 s | 16.93 s | 7 | |
| 2 | this branch | 43.94 | 26.13 s | 25.22 s | 9 | 18 ms, 16 ms |
| 3 | this branch | 45.42 | 59.82 s | 57.53 s | 9 | 70 ms, 16 ms |
| 4 | base | 53.21 | 75.99 s | 72.67 s | 7 | |

Owning directory, `pnpm test extensions/memory-core/src/memory`: 405.93 s wall (shard 403.83 s), 911 passed, 23 skipped, at a 1-minute load of 56.96 (`gates-final/cost/owning-dir.out`).

The host was shared with unrelated builds during these runs. Transform is 95 to 97 percent of each file's duration and the wall time of the same arm varies by up to 4 times, so the file walls do not separate the arms; the new cases themselves take 16 to 70 ms. Each new case opens four in-memory databases with three rows each and runs ten searches. CI seconds are not available before the PR runs.

## Gaps, stated plainly

- `pnpm changed:lanes --json` returns `extensions: true, extensionTests: true` and every other lane false. The owning directory and the out-of-directory consumers of the search worker ran anyway. Unrelated suites were not run.
- The two `check:changed` failures are in files outside this diff and reproduce on a clean checkout of the base.
- The real stores went through the built production search function with the built reader layer and statement cache, not through the Gateway: the Gateway and agent opener refuse these schema 24 snapshots without `doctor --fix`. The Gateway and CLI runs used the synthetic store. The counts match across both routes (4 recompiles and 3 registrations per search before, 0 after admission).
- The re-prepare itself is observed through authorizer callbacks during compilation, from a preload; `node:sqlite` exposes no reprepare counter. The Gateway timing ran on a busy host and is supporting evidence only.
- A `DatabaseSync` object that is closed and then reopened with `open()` would keep its registry entry without the functions. A repository search finds no production caller of `open()` on a connection object other than the reopen wrapper that `openNodeSqliteDatabase` installs; the existing per-connection `loadedExtensions` memo makes the same assumption. In production code the two SQL function names appear only in `manager-search.ts` (`gates-final/grep-checks.out`).
- One host, macOS only. Real stores use `unicode61`; `trigram` is covered by a synthetic store and the existing tests.
- Out of scope: other statements that bind a bare `LIMIT ?`, including Kysely `.limit(n)`, which compiles to `limit ?`. They re-prepare on every run for the same reason and would need their own change at the statement owner.

auto_merge.commit_message:
- Register the two memory search SQL functions once per connection; each
  search sets the matcher state their closures read. Replacing a function
  expired every prepared statement on the connection.
- Bind search LIMIT values and LIKE patterns as `LIMIT +?` and
  `LIKE (? || '')`. SQLite 3.47+ recompiles a statement on every run when a
  bare bound LIMIT or LIKE pattern reaches the planner.
- Test: sequential and interleaved searches on one connection register each
  function once, search SQL has no bare `LIMIT ?` or `LIKE ?`, and results
  equal a fresh connection.
- Update the four pinned keyword statement hashes in
  manager-search-worker.sqlite.test.ts for the rewritten SQL text.

prs.title: fix(feishu): stop inbound mentions from cascading into replies
prs.body:
Closes #121921

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Feishu group replies would automatically mention every non-bot participant mentioned in the inbound message, even when the agent's reply did not request those mentions. Error and fallback replies could therefore wake multiple bots and create an unintended cascade.

## Why This Change Was Made

Inbound mention targets remain available as agent context, but they are no longer passed into the reply dispatcher or automatically attached to generated replies. Explicit outbound mentions, native Feishu `at` rendering, and bot-authored required mentions (`requiredMentionTargets`) remain unchanged.

This restores the boundary introduced by #71396 without reverting the native mention-rendering improvements from #93522.

## User Impact

Feishu users and multi-agent groups no longer receive unrequested `@` notifications from ordinary, error, fallback, card, streaming, block, or chunked replies. Agents can still explicitly mention users when the outbound content or message-tool request asks for it.

## Evidence

- Regression coverage verifies non-streaming final/error replies, static cards, streaming card closes, and independent block/chunk delivery do not inherit inbound mention targets.
- Existing coverage verifies `requiredMentionTargets` still reaches every required text chunk and static card reply.
- Focused Feishu tests pass:
  - `reply-dispatcher.test.ts`: **124/124**
  - `bot.test.ts` + `send.test.ts`: **131/131**
  - Total: **255/255**
- `oxfmt --check` passes for all 3 changed files.
- Focused `oxlint` passes for all 3 changed files.
- `git diff --check` passes.

prs.title: fix(agent-core): bound runaway loops with turn/error-batch/idle-repeat guards (#120962)
prs.body: Closes #120962 [AI-assisted] ## What Problem This Solves Fixes an issue where a worker agent could enter an unbounded retry loop inside the native runLoop: an external service returning HTTP 429 (masked inside a "successful" tool output) drove 219 assistant turns / 177 tool calls / ~15M tokens over 6h42m, stopped only by the global `stuckSessionAbortMs` timeout rather than by any active guardrail. ## Why This Change Was Made Adds three opt-in hard cutoffs to the agent-core runLoop, each activating independently when set to a positive integer in `tools.loopDetection`: - **`turnLimit`** — max assistant turns per run; ends gracefully with a terminal message instead of another provider request. - **`maxConsecutiveErrorBatches`** — max consecutive all-error tool batches; any success resets the streak. - **`maxIdleRepeatCalls`** — max consecutive identical tool calls (same name + args); catches errors hidden inside successful output. Steering-skipped calls are excluded. `enabled: true` alone does not engage hard cutoffs (preserves upgrade contract). `enabled: false` disables both layers. Resolved config propagates through sessions, compaction, and worker launch descriptors. The launcher fences guard-enabled turns on worker bundles lacking the `worker-loop-guard-v1` capability; configless and `enabled:false` turns are unaffected. ## User Impact Operators who want the guardrails set at least one guard key (e.g. `turnLimit: 200`) in a `tools.loopDetection` block. Existing configurations gain no new hard termination behavior unless a guard key is explicitly set. Public package consumers see no change unless they opt in. ## Evidence **Focused tests (all pass):** - `packages/agent-core/src/agent-loop.guard.test.ts` — 23 tests: maxTurns, error-batch, idle-repeat, steering-skip exclusion (sequential + parallel), steering requeue - `src/agents/sessions/agent-session-loop-guard-transport.test.ts` — real `AgentSession` through local HTTP/SSE transport, 3 repeated calls → graceful termination, no 4th request - `src/agents/tool-loop-detection-config.test.ts` — 9 tests: per-key activation, `enabled:false` kill switch, per-agent cascade - `src/gateway/worker-environments/worker-turn-launcher.loop-guard.test.ts` — 6 tests: launcher fence, serialization, guard-off compatibility - `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/worker-admission.test.ts` — 25 tests: loop-guard capability in worker protocol features

prs.title: fix(sessions): context token count stays stale for the whole of a long agent turn
prs.body:
Related: #164550

## What Problem This Solves

The session's context count (`totalTokens`) can stay at its pre-turn value throughout a long embedded agent turn. This change publishes the latest settled model call's prompt context while the turn is running, so status readers can follow it. Turn completion still writes the final accounting result.

Current head: [`7f9e238a3d8871192affc39b7efe064d2bad37bf`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/7f9e238a3d8871192affc39b7efe064d2bad37bf). This adds the real-admission fixture repair to `5125da02158281f58db57ec2a10f73e67895d0e3`, which merged the previous PR head `05f287abc9ff40686a2a7e0d7c696e38ba646643` with upstream `fa3b107c37d3870510430037e902037110916a81`. Production code and Goal accounting policy are unchanged by the follow-up. Earlier measurements are retained with their original revisions.

## User Impact

The embedded runner publishes each available settled context snapshot. The latest snapshot can replace a larger one. The writer serialises writes, fences them to the admitted session/run, and drains before final accounting. Detached and incognito attempts, and follow-ups that preserve user-facing session state, do not use this writer. [Writer and eligibility checks](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/7f9e238a3d8871192affc39b7efe064d2bad37bf/src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-context-total-tokens.ts).

Goal accounting retains its existing peak-usage policy. The store-backed test starts a Goal with a 50,000-token budget, publishes 40,000, then 60,000, then 30,000 tokens. Current context finishes at 30,000; Goal usage remains 60,000 and `budget_limited`. The test publishes a lower snapshot through the real writer and store; it does not execute the compactor. [Exact assertions](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/7f9e238a3d8871192affc39b7efe064d2bad37bf/src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-context-total-tokens.test.ts#L115-L147).

Maintainer decision needed: should Goal usage retain that 60,000 peak after context falls to 30,000? My recommendation is to preserve that policy in this change. Crediting the Goal after compaction changes budget semantics and needs an explicit owner decision. No such approval is claimed here.

## Why This Change Was Made

The per-call subscriber and fenced writer make context visible before turn completion. Final accounting must still supersede intermediate values, including an explicitly unknown final context.

The October 19 integration carries `contextTotalsAccounted` through the current cron writer's closed operation and clears it only after the acknowledged write. The real SQLite-backed test covers both numeric and unknown final context while preserving a concurrent label change. prs.title: refactor(ui): reuse cron owner validation and payloads
prs.body:
Automations repeated the cron owner's page and cursor validator, then reparsed payloads that the storage owner had already admitted. The UI now uses `src/cron/service/list-page-validation.ts` for inventory reads and consumes each admitted job payload directly. This also removes a full-list filter allocation.

The payload guarantee is established by `getInvalidPersistedCronJobReason` in `src/cron/persisted-shape.ts`, enforced by `rowToCronJob` and `loadedCronStoreFromRows` before the Gateway's full list/get/update read views. Compact-row validation remains because it checks additional presentation fields. Snapshot changes, pagination consistency, request scope, and mutation preconditions keep their existing checks.

One obsolete 13-line test supplied a payload-less job that the producer rejects; the storage-boundary malformed-row proof remains. No markup, CSS, host tags, selectors, routes, or lazy registration changed.

| Proof | Result |
| --- | --- |
| UI typecheck | Passed |
| Cron controller, PR automation, and form suggestions | 78 tests passed across 3 files, once each |
| Scoped lint and format | Passed |
| Import cycles | Passed; 0 cycles |
| Production Knip | Passed |
| Independent review | No actionable P0–P2 findings |
| Base/head UI builds and strict performance | Both passed |
| Startup JavaScript gzip | 326,298 B → 326,301 B (+3 B); raw bytes unchanged at 980,991 |
| Startup CSS requests | 1 → 1 |
| Production LOC, seven touched source files | 1,469 → 1,397 (−72) |
| Test LOC | −13 |
| Solid checklist | Controllers/effects/render effects/untrack/listeners/queries/flush/owner calls: all 0 → 0 |

Base: `47bc52e9095c357fdb8b2c4271c497ad70f2f83b`. Broad runtime proof runs through `ci:full` PR CI. Local proof used the default pinned runtime; no local E2E suite ran.

CI attribution: run `39334686538` fails only `device-platform-family.real-gateway.e2e.test.ts` → “keeps signed browser identities while rendering fresh and legacy Mac and iPad labels” and `device-alias-rename.real-gateway.e2e.test.ts` → “persists a Devices-page alias rename through the real Gateway across reload and restart.” Both exact names reproduce on this PR’s merge base `47bc52e9095c357fdb8b2c4271c497ad70f2f83b`: 2 failed files / 2 failed tests, exit 1, identical `DeviceIdentityStorageError` for noncanonical fixture paths. The relevant test, helper, identity owner, and dependency blobs are identical between the merge base and CI checkout `92c566bf56a07baccd98e3a47e30dbe380507b57`. All other selected CI jobs, including security-fast and remaining UI E2E, passed or intentionally skipped. These two fixture failures are retained under the documented inherited-failure route; the scheduled-main failures were different and were not used as matching evidence.

prs.title: fix: CLI auth status/probe path regression
prs.body:
## Summary

Found one regression in the CLI auth status/probe path. The commit intentionally makes unscoped external CLI discovery skip missing runtime-only profiles, but `models status` and `models status --probe` still load the auth store without passing the providers they are about to report or probe.

## What ClawSweeper Is Fixing

- **Medium: `models status --probe` misses CLI-only credentials after scoped discovery** (regression)
  - File: `src/commands/models/list.probe.ts:259`
  - Evidence: `src/agents/auth-profiles/external-cli-sync.ts:210` now returns false for unscoped missing external CLI profiles unless a matching stored OAuth profile already exists. `buildProbeTargets` still calls `ensureAuthProfileStore(agentDir)` without `allowKeychainPrompt: false`, `externalCliProviderIds`, or `externalCliProfileIds`, even though the function receives the exact `providers` and probe profile filters at `src/commands/models/list.probe.ts:254-256`. A focused smoke with a temporary Codex CLI auth file confirmed `resolveExternalCliAuthProfiles(emptyStore)` returns `[]`, while `resolveExternalCliAuthProfiles(emptyStore, { providerIds: ["openai-codex"] })` returns `["openai-codex:default"]`.
  - Impact: A user who only has file-backed Codex/Claude/Minimax CLI credentials and no persisted OpenClaw auth profile can resolve runtime auth through the newly scoped model-auth path, but `openclaw models status --probe` will build no profile target for that same credential. This produces false “nothing to probe” or missing-auth diagnostics for the provider most likely being checked.
  - Suggested fix: In `buildProbeTargets`, load the store with a scope derived from the requested probe surface, for example `ensureAuthProfileStore(agentDir, { allowKeychainPrompt: false, config: cfg, externalCliProviderIds: providers, externalCliProfileIds: options.profileIds })`. The plain status path at `src/commands/models/list.status-command.ts:223` should likewise pass the config-derived external CLI scope, matching `src/gateway/server-methods/models-auth-status.ts:296-301`.
  - Confidence: high

## Expected Repair Surface

- `src/agents/auth-profiles.external-cli-scope.test.ts`
- `src/agents/auth-profiles.external-cli-sync.test.ts`

prs.body:
## Summary
- Honor `messages.suppressToolErrors` before mutating-tool warning generation.
- Preserve existing `sessions_send`, exec-timeout detail, and explicit `suppressToolErrorWarnings` behavior.
- Add regression coverage for mutating tool errors plus an Unreleased changelog entry.

Existing related PR: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/81561 covers the same issue, but its Real behavior proof check is failing because the proof fields do not match the current parser contract. This PR keeps the fix narrow and includes the required proof fields below.

## Verification
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/pi-embedded-runner/run/payloads.errors.test.ts`
- `node --import tsx -e 'import { buildEmbeddedRunPayloads } from "./src/agents/pi-embedded-runner/run/payloads.ts"; const payloads = buildEmbeddedRunPayloads({ assistantTexts: [], toolMetas: [], lastAssistant: undefined, isCronTrigger: false, sessionKey: "agent:main:telegram:group:-1003998880259:topic:1", inlineToolResultsAllowed: false, verboseLevel: "off", reasoningLevel: "off", toolResultFormat: "plain", lastToolError: { toolName: "write", error: "connection timeout" }, config: { messages: { suppressToolErrors: true } } }); console.log(JSON.stringify({scenario:"mutating write tool error with messages.suppressToolErrors=true", payloadCount: payloads.length, payloadTexts: payloads.map((p) => p.text)}, null, 2));'`
- `git diff --check HEAD~2..HEAD`

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: When `messages.suppressToolErrors=true`, mutating tool failures such as write/message/apply-patch failures should not emit separate user-facing warning bubbles.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw source checkout on the Phaedrus VPS, using the Telegram session key shape from the observed failing group chat.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: Ran the payload builder directly with a mutating `write` tool failure, `messages.suppressToolErrors=true`, and a Telegram group session key:

```bash
node --import tsx -e 'import { buildEmbeddedRunPayloads } from "./src/agents/pi-embedded-runner/run/payloads.ts"; const payloads = buildEmbeddedRunPayloads({ assistantTexts: [], toolMetas: [], lastAssistant: undefined, isCronTrigger: false, sessionKey: "agent:main:telegram:group:-1003998880259:topic:1", inlineToolResultsAllowed: false, verboseLevel: "off", reasoningLevel: "off", toolResultFormat: "plain", lastToolError: { toolName: "write", error: "connection timeout" }, config: { messages: { suppressToolErrors: true } } }); console.log(JSON.stringify({scenario:"mutating write tool error with messages.suppressToolErrors=true", payloadCount: payloads.length, payloadTexts: payloads.map((p) => p.text)}, null, 2));'
```

Evidence after fix:

```json
{
  "scenario": "mutating write tool error with messages.suppressToolErrors=true",
  "payloadCount": 0,
  "payloadTexts": []
}
```

Observed result after fix: The mutating tool failure produced zero outbound payloads, so no Telegram warning bubble would be delivered when `messages.suppressToolErrors` is enabled.

What was not tested: I did not deploy this branch into the live root-owned OpenClaw install on Phaedrus; live Telegram validation will happen after this PR is merged/released or otherwise deployed.

prs.title: fix: retire timed-out Codex app-server clients
prs.body:
## Summary
- retire the shared Codex app-server client when an OpenClaw app-server turn hits the attempt/idle timeout
- bound abort-time `turn/interrupt` requests to 5s so stuck Codex turns cannot leave a poisoned client around
- add regression coverage for closing a timed-out client before the next Discord turn reuses it

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: Discord-backed Codex agents could time out an OpenClaw app-server attempt, leave the Codex app-server child alive and CPU-spinning, then reuse that poisoned client on the next mention.

Real environment tested: local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, Codex app-server extension runtime/test lane, using the same OpenClaw wrapper code path that owns Discord ClawSweeper app-server attempts.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
```bash
pnpm format:check extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.test.ts CHANGELOG.md
pnpm tsgo:extensions:test
node scripts/test-projects.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

Evidence after fix: terminal output from the focused extension run after this patch:
```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  93 passed (93)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 36.94s
```
The new regression drives a turn that accepts `turn/start`, never emits completion, hits the attempt timeout, sends `turn/interrupt` with `{ timeoutMs: 5000 }`, closes the app-server client, and releases the active session.

Observed result after fix: the wrapper now retires the timed-out app-server client instead of keeping it eligible for reuse, so a follow-up Discord mention gets a fresh Codex app-server process rather than the CPU-spinning one from the timed-out attempt.

What was not tested: live Hetzner/Discord repro after this branch; the live failure was observed before the patch, and this PR proves the OpenClaw wrapper timeout boundary locally.

## Test plan
- `pnpm format:check extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.test.ts CHANGELOG.md`
- `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test`
- `node scripts/test-projects.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`

## Summary

- Pin the OpenAI API-key onboarding default model (`openai/gpt-5.5`) to the PI runtime.
- Preserve any existing explicit runtime override for that model.
- Add regression coverage and a changelog entry for #79358.

## Root Cause

Fresh OpenAI API-key setup saved credentials into the `openai:default` auth profile, but the official `openai/*` model path can be routed through the implicit Codex harness when no model-scoped runtime is set. That harness path does not consume the saved `openai:default` profile, so requests could go out without the expected Authorization header even though onboarding had written an API-key profile.

## User Impact

Fresh API-key installs now use the saved OpenAI profile for the default `openai/gpt-5.5` model instead of falling into the implicit Codex harness path.

Fixes #79358. Thanks @pubnub-mrruby.

## Summary

Describe the problem and fix in 2-5 bullets:

If this PR fixes a plugin beta-release blocker, title it `fix(<plugin-id>): beta blocker - <summary>` and link the matching `Beta blocker: <plugin-name> - <summary>` issue labeled `beta-blocker`. Contributors cannot label PRs, so the title is the PR-side signal for maintainers and automation.

- Problem: OpenClaw label colors currently use saturated colors for routine taxonomy labels, so channels, plugins, apps, areas, impacts, priorities, and automation gates compete visually.
- Why it matters: Maintainers scanning large issue and PR lists need saturated colors to mean urgency or action, not ordinary categorization.
- What changed: Added `scripts/sync-openclaw-label-colors.mjs`, a dry-run-by-default GitHub label color migration script that updates colors only, preserves label names/descriptions, and reports changes by label family. Also updated `scripts/sync-labels.ts` so future labels created from `.github/labeler.yml` inherit the quieter family palette.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): This PR does not edit live labels by itself, rename labels, change descriptions, or alter labeler path rules.

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)

prs.title: refactor(ui): reuse catalog reader on Agents page
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Agents overview duplicated the catalog reader's request cancellation, cache subscription, and publication subscription. It now uses `ModelCatalogReader`, retaining the page's panel error presentation and one pending Gateway-recovery intent. The reader passes the original error to its callback; existing callers can continue to ignore it.

Selection, connection, and disposal still clear the reader. A Gateway that resumes while a request is pending waits for its result before retrying a failure. The canonical model-catalog publication/invalidation path is unchanged. File-list snapshots stay local because an open editor must retain its list and drafts while the canonical cache is invalidated and rebuilt.

## Evidence

| Proof | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `pnpm tsgo:ui` | Pass |
| Agents page and file lifecycle | 39 tests passed |
| Model catalog recovery | 5 tests passed |
| Focused lint and formatting | Pass |

| Production Knip | Pass |

Production LOC in the two touched files: **1,319 → 1,260 (−59)**. Tests: unchanged. No markup, styles, routes, or selectors changed, so no visual screenshots are applicable. The existing max-lines exception remains necessary for the Agents state file; no allowance was raised.

Build comparison: base `2ccb5e7b30d859798889f68315f5337d7264cf0c`, head `9c096eeee17aea2d2aa60d51b3e40db5cc71c22d`, with identical fixed build identity on the same machine. Both pass the current 338,900 B startup ceiling. No lazy boundary or eager dependency import changes. `ci:full` covers the shared reader consumers.


Exact-head CI run [39336729073](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39336729073) passed all UI unit shards, all nine regular UI E2E shards, type/lint/guard checks, and startup performance. Its two failing real-Gateway tests also fail in the latest completed scheduled main run [39335414307](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39335414307):

- `Control UI browser platform family with a real Gateway > keeps signed browser identities while rendering fresh and legacy Mac and iPad labels`
- `Control UI device alias rename with a real Gateway > persists a Devices-page alias rename through the real Gateway across reload and restart`

Both runs report `DeviceIdentityStorageError` because the fixtures use an identity path outside the canonical client credentials database. CI tested merge `1c98dad26b6c8c7ec6627f390e3a4e2753ef9e5c` with parents `50520de188dd2c498db8bd397d0ceb932ba794e4` and reviewed head `9c096eeee17aea2d2aa60d51b3e40db5cc71c22d`.
