prs.title: fix(gateway): the dispatcher tick must not serve a frozen mixed revision (content-based skew gate)
prs.body:
## What

A checkout rewrite that lands under a long-lived service must never leave that service serving a
**mixed revision**. `sys.path` / `sys.modules` are per-process, so the writer cannot reach a
consumer that is already running: the enforceable half lives in the **consumer**, and the first
consumer is the kanban dispatcher's tick.

## Why the signal must be CONTENT, not the ref

`gateway.code_skew.detect_code_skew()` fingerprints only `.git/HEAD` → ref → sha and never reads the
working tree. An interrupted merge leaves `HEAD` at the pre-merge commit and the recovery restores
paths "to HEAD", so a **working-tree** rewrite under an unchanged `HEAD` is invisible to it.
Measured on a live host: `detect_code_skew()` returned `None` while 120+ paths differed from HEAD,
a gateway kept serving a patched `hermes_cli/*` beside an unpatched `agent/*`, and every spawn died
`cannot import name 'ADVISORY_SKILLS_ENV' from 'agent.skill_commands'` for hours **after** the disk
was repaired. A ref-only guard is blind to exactly that window.

## What lands

* **`hermes_cli/tree_fingerprint.py` (new).** One bounded digest over the `.py` set of the package
  trees a process loads (`relpath` + `size` + content `sha256`, sorted; `__pycache__` excluded).
  Recorded once at boot, re-checked later. Cheap on the happy path: memoized on a stat-only
  signature, so a repeat check is one stat walk and bytes are re-read only when something moved.
  `mtime_ns` is deliberately not in the digest — a byte-identical restore (a `git checkout`, a
  re-applied patch) is not drift. Every uncertain read returns `None`: the guard **fails open**,
  like the ref guard it backs up.
* **`gateway/code_skew`** — the existing gateway boot carrier records the content half too
  (`record_boot_fingerprint()`), and `detect_content_skew()` exposes it.
* **The consumer is the dispatch tick.** `kanban_db_dispatch.dispatch_once` consults the gate
  **once per tick, before any spawn**, so the gateway's embedded dispatcher, the standalone daemon
  and the CLI `dispatch` verb all share it and none of them is a hole. On proven skew the tick
  spawns nothing and returns a **non-green** result:
  * a `tree-skew-yield: …` reason on `DispatchResult` (never `idle`, never a silent green — the
    `CronTickYielded` precedent),
  * a machine-global status record a human reads (`<kanban_home>/kanban/dispatcher_tick_yield.json`),
  * a `WARNING` on the gateway's dispatcher loop,
  * and **exactly ONE** acting card, idempotency-keyed
    `<boot-fingerprint>:<boot-pid>:<window-start>` — deterministic, no model, no prose a reader has
    to interpret. The key is stable for the life of the frozen process, so N ticks resolve to one card.
* **The clean path is unchanged:** a coherent tree, a byte-identical rewrite, an unreadable tree and
  a process that never recorded a boot fingerprint all proceed.

Cost is **O(tick), never O(cards)**: one check per tick, asserted by test. The spawn path is
deliberately *not* made lazy/tolerant — a mixed tree must refuse by name rather than keep spawning
half a revision (silent wrong behaviour is worse than a named refusal).

## Tests

`tests/hermes_cli/test_kanban_dispatch_tree_skew_gate.py` (14 tests, all green):

* a **working-tree edit with HEAD unchanged is DETECTED** — the case a ref-only guard fails by
  construction, with the ref probe asserted blind in the same test;
* HEAD-only drift is detected (the ref half rides along as a fast path);
* a clean tree, a byte-identical rewrite, an unreadable tree and a record-less process are **not**
  refused (no false positive);
* N ticks on a skewed tree file **exactly one** acting card, keyed `<fingerprint>:<pid>:<window>`;
* the non-green status record exists, names both fingerprints, and is retired by the process that
  recorded it (a foreign process's marker is never cleared by a sibling);
* the check runs **once per tick**, not per card, and the steady state does not re-read file bytes.

Also covered: `tests/hermes_cli/test_code_skew.py`, `tests/hermes_cli/test_kanban_dispatch_tick_hook.py`.

## Notes for review

* This branch is based on `main` at the time of writing. The live host also carries this change
  inline, where two helpers are shared with an in-flight substrate-guard change rather than
  redefined; here they are self-contained (`_tick_yield_*`) so this PR does not depend on that one.
  The live tree additionally retires a foreign marker whose recorder is *proven dead*; that clause
  needs the liveness-witness substrate and is deliberately not part of this commit.
* Draft: opened for review, not for merge.

prs.title: fix(terminal): a posix_spawn local handle must satisfy the registry's process-handle contract
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Makes the local backend's POSIX spawn path safe to hand to the process registry, and puts the
process-handle contract under the type checker so the next omission of this kind fails a check
instead of production.

Two things ride together, because the second is the guardrail for the first.

**1. The posix_spawn handle was not Popen-shaped enough for the registry's teardown (the bug).**
When a foreground command yields to the background (the user sends a message mid-command),
`tools/terminal_tool_background.py` hands the live handle to `process_registry.adopt_local`.
Finishing that adopted session runs `_release_finished_handles`, which released every stream of the
handle — including `proc.stderr`, an attribute the posix_spawn class never set (its wiring is
`stdout=PIPE, stderr=STDOUT`, i.e. the child's stderr is dup2'd onto the stdout pipe). Two
consequences, one cause:

* the reader thread that finishes the adopted session died inside `_publish_finished` — visible in
  the gateway log as `[gateway-crash] thread proc-reader-<id> raised AttributeError` — losing the
  completion notice;
* the session stayed in `_finished`, so every later spawn's `_track_started → _prune_if_needed`
  re-raised on it and `terminal(background=true)` answered
  `Failed to start background process: '_PosixSpawnProcess' object has no attribute 'stderr'` for
  the life of the process. Backgrounding was unusable, not degraded.

The fix is `stderr = None` — exactly what `Popen(stdout=PIPE, stderr=STDOUT)` reports — so the
handle stays Popen-shaped for every consumer that duck-types one, plus releasing the streams through
`getattr`: that teardown is best-effort by contract and runs on the reader thread and inside the
prune path, so a handle missing an optional stream must degrade to "nothing to close" rather than
wedge every later spawn.

**2. The contract is now typed, which is what should have caught it.**
`_run_bash` was annotated with a private union of two concrete classes while both of its consumers
spoke `subprocess.Popen`: `adopt_local` took a Popen and `ProcessSession.process` was
`Optional[Popen]`. On the POSIX path the handle is `_PosixSpawnProcess`, which is not a Popen, so
the checker had nothing to compare and the registry's teardown read an attribute the handle never
declared. `ProcessHandle` (`tools/environments/base_output.py`) is now the one contract all three
sites speak, and it declares the members consumers already read: `stderr` and `stdin` beside the
`stdout`/`returncode`/`poll`/`wait`/`kill` it had, plus `pid`, which the registry records on the
session and fingerprints before signalling the process group. A backend with no separate stream or
host pid of its own must still DECLARE it, as `None`, never omit it.

The branch also carries the spawn itself and the `close_fds` preservation on that path (its first
two commits) so the whole local-bash spawn change is reviewable in one place.

## Related Issue

No upstream issue exists — the failure was found and reproduced on our own install (a
`_PosixSpawnProcess` background spawn); repro was a foreground command that yields to the
background. Happy to file an issue if you would rather the fix be tracked against one.

Related prior art in this repo, checked before opening: #70577 (closed) took a posix_spawn route
for the macOS fork() deadlock, and #34789 (merged) fixed the same reader thread dying on an fd-less
stdout. Neither covers a handle that reaches `process_registry.adopt_local` without the attributes
its teardown reads.

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)

## Changes Made

- `tools/environments/local.py` — spawn local bash with `os.posix_spawn` instead of fork+exec on
  POSIX (a `_PosixSpawnProcess` handle implementing the same drain interface), with `close_fds`
  semantics preserved on that path by explicit inherited-fd close actions and a fork+exec fallback
  when the spawn itself raises `OSError`. `_PosixSpawnProcess` exposes `stderr = None` and closes it
  with the other streams; `_run_bash` returns the declared `ProcessHandle` contract instead of the
  private union; `_force_kill_process` skips the process-group path for a handle with no host pid.
- `tools/process_registry.py` — `adopt_local` and `ProcessSession.process` are typed against
  `ProcessHandle`; `_release_finished_handles` releases streams through `getattr`; the host-pid
  terminate path short-circuits a handle with no host pid.
- `tools/environments/base_output.py` — `ProcessHandle` declares `stderr`, `stdin` and `pid` beside
  its existing members; `_ThreadedProcessHandle` declares the same three as `None` (the shape
  `Popen(stdout=PIPE, stderr=STDOUT, stdin=DEVNULL)` reports), so the SDK adapters satisfy the
  contract rather than going unchecked.
- `tools/terminal_tool_background.py` — the yield handler that calls `adopt_local` is annotated, so
  the handoff is checked at both ends.
- `tests/tools/test_local_env_posix_spawn.py` (new) — child descriptor and session-leader coverage
  for the spawn path, plus `TestSpawnHandleIsPopenShaped`, which fails on the pre-fix tree with the
  production traceback.
- `tests/tools/test_local_env_cwd_recovery.py` — updated for the new spawn path.

## How to Test

1. Regression tests, run at the branch tip (macOS 26, CPython 3.11):

   ```
   python -m pytest tests/tools/test_local_env_posix_spawn.py tests/tools/test_process_registry.py \
       tests/tools/test_local_env_cwd_recovery.py -q
   → 106 passed, 20 skipped
   ```

2. A/B on the regression itself (the new tests fail on the pre-fix tree with the production
   traceback, and pass at the tip):

   ```
   git checkout <base> -- tools/environments/local.py tools/process_registry.py
   python -m pytest tests/tools/test_local_env_posix_spawn.py -q
   → AttributeError: '_PosixSpawnProcess' object has no attribute 'stderr'
     at tools/process_registry.py:1658 (and at the handle's own stream check)
   git checkout <tip> -- tools/environments/local.py tools/process_registry.py   # tree clean again
   ```

3. The typing guard, measured rather than asserted: delete `self.stderr = None` from
   `_PosixSpawnProcess` and run pyright over the touched modules —

   ```
   Type "Popen[Any] | _PosixSpawnProcess" is not assignable to return type "ProcessHandle"
     "_PosixSpawnProcess" is incompatible with protocol "ProcessHandle"
       "stderr" is not present
   ```

   i.e. the omission now fails a check at the contract boundary instead of in a production
   teardown.

4. `pyright --pythonversion 3.11 tools/environments/base_output.py tools/environments/base.py
   tools/environments/local.py tools/process_registry.py tools/terminal_tool_background.py`
   → 4 fewer diagnostics than the base revision and none added (the remaining ones in those files
   are pre-existing: an `Optional` narrowing in `base.py`'s kill/waiter callers, and
   `_pipe_stdin`'s private bookkeeping attributes).

## Checklist

### Code

- [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)
- [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate
- [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix
- [x] I've run `python -m pytest tests/tools/test_local_env_posix_spawn.py tests/tools/test_process_registry.py tests/tools/test_local_env_cwd_recovery.py -q` and all tests pass (106 passed, 20 skipped)
- [x] I've added tests for my changes
- [x] I've tested on my platform: macOS (the posix_spawn path is POSIX-only; Windows keeps the
      unchanged `Popen` route)

### Documentation & Housekeeping

- [ ] I've updated relevant documentation — N/A. Internal handle contract; no user-visible
      behaviour, flag, tool schema or config key changes.
- [ ] I've updated `cli-config.yaml.example` — N/A, no config change.
- [ ] I've updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `AGENTS.md` — N/A.
- [x] I've considered cross-platform impact (Windows, macOS) — the new spawn path is gated on
      `not _IS_WINDOWS` and every POSIX failure falls back to the existing fork+exec route; the pgid
      and descriptor work is unchanged on Windows.
- [ ] I've updated tool descriptions/schemas — N/A, no tool surface change.

prs.title: fix(kanban): a mass-crash reclaim sweep must ABORT and fail loud (R4/R6 of ruling t_63a20c59)
prs.body:
## R4 — a mass-crash sweep must ABORT and fail loud

Ruling `t_63a20c59` (platform-stl, 2026-10-10). A reclaim sweep that would close **>= 3 runs in ONE
tick** is a host-systemic signature, not N card failures — a broken liveness witness, not N broken
cards. The reclaim path now decides **before it writes**: `>= 3` unexplained-death closures at one
instant refuses the whole write (no run ended, no claim released, nothing counted) and fails loud
with a deterministic `count` + `ended_at` signature, per-card evidence events, and one idempotent
acting card for the design authority. Outcome is a loud card, never a silent board mutation; the
count guard is reversible via `KANBAN_MASS_CRASH_ABORT_THRESHOLD` (a value < 2 disables it).

**The measured census this exists for.** All 21 `crashed` runs on the migrations board fell into
three instants (`ended_at` 14:20:37 ×8, 13:35:34 ×5, 00:01:23 ×8) and every one carried
`pid N not alive`. pid 70697 was measured ALIVE eight minutes after the 14:20:37 sweep and still
writing the live tree. Not one of the 21 was a genuine crash.

**Which closures are counted.** Only the *unexplained-death* family (`unknown` / `nonzero_exit` /
`signaled`) — the class a bad liveness evaluation can forge. A protocol violation (clean exit,
paperwork skipped), a terminal provider refusal and a rate-limited requeue carry their own evidence
and their own bounded budget; counting them would refuse a legitimate sweep of N cards whose workers
each finished successfully.

## R6 — the deployed identity generation is checked, not assumed

The shape the dispatcher **writes** is stamped on disk on the first tick and compared on every later
tick: an interpreter move, a lost `psutil`, or witness bytes dropped by a tree write is detected in
**ONE tick** and alerts (the recurring class: `t_1e6a58c3`, 2026-09-26, 2026-09-29, `t_ae80d242`,
2026-10-10 — each fix previously lived as an override or an in-memory build).

The same comparison is made against the fingerprints actually **read** off running rows: a row whose
fingerprint was built by a different identity generation is HELD — not reclaimed, not counted, its
claim untouched (R2's `UNKNOWN -> HOLD` at row granularity). Three incomparable shapes were measured
in circulation at once: the empty-reference absolute-epoch form, the `unverified` marker, and
`bootsession:<uuid>|<ref>|<start>`. A row with no fingerprint or an `unverified` marker keeps the
existing bare-existence rule, so no pre-fingerprint card is stranded.

## Tests

37 new tests, all green; the 2026-10-10 three-instant census is the regression fixture. Acceptance is
covered end-to-end: a synthetic tick that would close 3 runs at one `ended_at` writes **nothing**
(statuses, pids, claims and runs all unchanged), and files one acting card plus one evidence event
per card. Neighbouring reclaim suites (`test_kanban_db`, `test_kanban_reclaim_claim_lock_guard`,
`test_kanban_core_functionality`, worker-lifecycle and reconcile suites): 116 passed, with the same
3 pre-existing environment failures present on a pristine `main` checkout.

## Blast radius / rollback

Refuses writes only. A wrong refusal is a loud, hourly-idempotent card and a `DispatchResult` field
(`crash_sweep_refused`, `crash_sweep_held`, `identity_generation_alerts`); rollback is to raise or
disable the threshold, or to re-record the generation stamp. No board data is touched by either.

prs.title: fix(cron): export the fire's occurrence identity to script and worker subprocesses
prs.body:
## Why

The scheduler is the only component that knows which OCCURRENCE a fire is, and it does not tell its
children. `cron/scheduler_script.py::_run_job_script` builds the child env from
`build_subprocess_env()` plus the interpreter overlay only, so a `no_agent` script — and the
restart-safe external worker — starts with no way to learn which occurrence it belongs to.

Re-deriving it inside the child is not possible in general: `cron/executions.py::create_execution`
records the SCHEDULER's pid, so a child cannot recognise its own ledger row, and selecting a row by
nearest window would be resolution logic in the consumer. Anything that must act on the slot it was
scheduled for (rather than on the wall clock it happened to start at) has no correct input today:
a held or catch-up fire is indistinguishable from an on-time one.

## What

`cron/execution_identity.py::cron_execution_env(job)` is one expression of that contract:

| variable | value |
|---|---|
| `HERMES_CRON_JOB_ID` | the job id |
| `HERMES_CRON_EXECUTION_ID` | the ledger execution id |
| `HERMES_CRON_SCHEDULED_INSTANT` | the occurrence fired, verbatim as the ledger holds it (UTC ISO-8601) |
| `HERMES_CRON_SOURCE` | the execution's source (`builtin` / `direct` / provider name) |

A value that is absent is **omitted** rather than exported empty: absence is the single readable
"off-schedule / manual fire" signal, and a present-but-empty variable is indistinguishable from a
real one. Only ids, an instant and a source travel — never a secret.

It is applied by `_run_job_script(identity=...)` AFTER `build_subprocess_env(...)` and the
interpreter overlay, because that sanitizer strips Hermes-owned names — an overlay applied earlier
would vanish. The same helper feeds the restart-safe worker's child env. The four values ride the
dispatched job snapshot, beside the `execution_id` / `_scheduled_instant` already carried there, and
the instant is passed through exactly as the ledger holds it: `cron/occurrences.py::scheduled_instant`
stays the only normaliser.

Callers with no fire (`cron/monitor.py`) pass no identity. Nothing reads these names yet, so the
change is additive and inert — no existing job's children change behaviour.

## Tests

New `tests/cron/test_cron_execution_env.py`:

* the helper's contract, including the omission rule (absent, never present-but-empty);
* a real tick of a real `no_agent` job whose script reports the env it received — the exported
  instant equals the ledger row's `scheduled_instant` (RED on the base: the variable is absent
  there);
* a manual run of a scheduled job (`manual_run_at`), whose ledger row has no `scheduled_instant`,
  where the variable is absent from the child env while the other three are present.

The rest of the cron suite is unchanged (`tests/cron/` run before and after: identical failure
inventory on the base tree apart from those three tests flipping red → green).

prs.title: kanban: name and classify spawn-seam substrate import failures (spawn seam guard)
prs.body:
## What

The spawn seam now **names** the artifact when a worker spawn dies on the dispatching tree's own
import inconsistency, and **classifies** that failure as substrate so it cannot kill a lane
silently.

The incident this addresses: every review-run worker spawn on our fleet died with
`cannot import name 'ADVISORY_SKILLS_ENV' from 'agent.skill_commands'` — an import no source file
contained — and the whole review lane went dead while each individual card looked like its own
problem. The stale `cpython-311` bytecode beside the tree was a smell, not the wound: CPython
selects `__pycache__/<mod>.<sys.implementation.cache_tag>.pyc`, so a 3.14 runtime cannot select a
3.11 pyc at all. The wound is a tree whose own modules disagree (importer present, provider
absent).

## Changes (`hermes_cli/kanban_db_dispatch.py`)

* `classify_spawn_failure(exc, *, tree)` — the ONE decider: `card` (default) | `substrate_import` |
  `host_capacity`. Both spawn-seam `except` sites (workspace resolution and the spawn call) go
  through it via `_record_spawn_failure`; no scattered `isinstance` checks.
* `describe_tree_import_failure(exc, *, tree, task_id)` — one line, front-loaded for the 500-char
  truncation `_record_task_failure` applies:

  ```
  tree-import-inconsistency: importer <relpath>:<lineno> imports <symbol>; provider <relpath>
  sha256=<64> mtime=<epoch> size=<n> defines-it=no differs-from-HEAD=yes; tree-self-consistent=no;
  foreign-tag-pyc-in-provider-dir=0; nothing of card <id> ran
  ```

  The importer frame comes from `traceback.extract_tb` (deepest frame under the tree); the provider
  is **resolved, never imported** (`importlib.util.find_spec`); `differs-from-HEAD` checks the
  `git show` exit status FIRST (a failed `git show` piped into a hash yields the empty-input
  digest, i.e. a difference that does not exist). Cost: failure path only.
* `substrate_import` ⇒ `infrastructure=True`: `consecutive_failures` does not move, the breaker
  does not trip, the card stays retryable, and `check_respawn_guard` spaces it with the new
  `substrate_cooldown` reason. That reason RETURNS either way — the naming line quotes module paths,
  so it can contain a word the quota/auth pattern matches (`agent/auth.py`) and `blocker_auth` would
  park the card forever on a failure that was never the card's.
* `_maybe_file_substrate_actor` — the lane-level half: count the DISTINCT cards carrying
  `substrate_import:<provider-relpath>:<symbol>` inside the cooldown window, per board, and at
  `kanban.failure_threshold` (no new config key; legacy `spawn_failure_threshold` honoured) file
  exactly ONE acting card, idempotency-keyed `substrate:<signature>:<board>:<window-start>`, event
  `substrate_actor_filed`, body = the recorded naming line + affected cards + tree evidence
  (`git status --porcelain`, provider sha/mtime). Deterministic; no LLM. The existing per-card
  `gave_up` is untouched.
* `sweep_tree_bytecode_pycs(tree)` / `_pyc_tag` — REPORT-only: sourceless `*.pyc` outside
  `__pycache__`, non-zero header flags / hash-based pycs, and the tag population (foreign tags are
  inert). **No spawn is ever gated on bytecode**: refusing on a foreign-tag population would be a
  false-positive spawn killer, the very failure mode this removes.

## Tests (`tests/hermes_cli/test_kanban_spawn_substrate_guard.py`, 7 cases)

1. a substrate import failure never charges the card (`consecutive_failures` unmoved, breaker
   untripped, `infrastructure`/`substrate_import`/`substrate_signature` on the run) and is spaced
   by `substrate_cooldown`; a control `RuntimeError` on the same card still spends budget;
2. the naming line carries importer `file:line`, provider path, sha256, size, `defines-it`,
   `differs-from-HEAD`, `tree-self-consistent` and the card id;
3. N cards on one signature ⇒ exactly ONE actor card, idempotent within the window, below the
   threshold nothing is filed;
4. proof-of-impossibility: a `cpython-311`/`cpython-99` pyc beside a module is never selected — the
   missing name still raises and the source symbol still wins;
5. the sweep reports sourceless pycs and non-zero flags while measuring foreign tags as inert;
6. the classifier keeps card-level failures, third-party imports and out-of-tree imports on the
   card;
7. the threshold follows `kanban.failure_threshold` (legacy alias honoured, non-positive ⇒ default).

`python -m pytest tests/hermes_cli/test_kanban_spawn_substrate_guard.py` → 7 passed.

## Notes

* `kanban_db_dispatch` still does not import the tree-skew fence module (pinned by a sibling suite);
  the tree root is derived from this module's own file.
* No new config keys. Apply-time and boot-time guards are out of scope (separate cards).

prs.title: fix(kanban): a board-scoped dispatch fence (board.json "dispatch": false)
prs.body:
## What

A **board-scoped dispatch fence**: a board whose `board.json` carries `"dispatch": false`
is never served by the kanban dispatcher, and the flag fails closed at BOTH gates the
dispatcher has.

* **enumeration** — `kanban_db.list_dispatch_boards()` is the dispatcher's own board
  list. It drops the fenced board, so `tick_once_for_board` is never called for it.
  `list_boards()` is unchanged: a fenced board stays VISIBLE in
  `hermes kanban boards list` / the dashboard — it is simply never spawned from.
* **the per-tick spawn guard** — `kanban_db_dispatch.dispatch_once()` resolves the board
  it is actually against (the `board=` kwarg, else the board the OPEN CONNECTION belongs
  to) and returns `DispatchResult(skipped_board_disabled=True)` **before** the tick lock,
  the reclaim phase and every claim. So a caller that bypasses enumeration — the CLI
  `hermes kanban --board <estate> dispatch` — still cannot spawn a card from it. A
  refused pass leaves the card `ready` with 0 runs and prints
  `Refused: board is NOT dispatch-enabled (estate/scratch board)`.

`board.json` gains `"dispatch"`, default **true at read time** (absent / `None` /
unrecognised = admitted), so every board that predates the key is unchanged and an
unrelated write does not materialise it. Set it at birth with
`hermes kanban boards create <slug> --no-dispatch`, or later with
`hermes kanban boards set-dispatch <slug> on|off`.

Also closed here, measured on a live worker: **archiving is not durable while a worker's
env pins its store path.** The pinned worker's next `connect()` mints an empty
`kanban.db` back at the archived slug's directory, which used to read as
`archived=False` and re-enter the dispatch set. `kanban_db.board_is_archived_stub()`
refuses to admit a minted directory sitting beside an `_archived/<slug>-<epoch>` copy —
including the board's own `archived` tombstone once a store has been minted beside it —
so a mint can no longer undo an archive. An explicit
`hermes kanban boards create <slug>` is the sanctioned re-admission.

## Why

Measured 2026-09-29: a SEV1/failure card redirected to a "scratch" board was spawned by
the fleet dispatcher (`~/.hermes/logs/gateway.log` 18:12:16
`kanban dispatcher [failure-acceptance-t4ffa46e3]: spawned=1`) at the reserved-tranche
priority 999000, while the board held 13 ready phantom cards. A redirect to a normal
board is not isolation: the dispatcher serves every non-archived board. This is the
board-level admission flag that makes a rehearsal/estate board safe BY CONSTRUCTION.

## Test plan

`tests/hermes_cli/test_kanban_estate_board_dispatch.py` (9 cases):

* a ready card on an estate board spawns NOTHING — `skipped_board_disabled is True`,
  `spawned == []`, the spy `spawn_fn` is NEVER called — with a negative control: the
  identical card shape on an unflagged board still spawns;
* the refusal holds when the tick names the board directly and when it is resolved off
  the connection (`HERMES_KANBAN_BOARD` pinned, no `board=` kwarg);
* `_KanbanDispatcher.tick_once()` visits the live board and never the estate one;
* `list_dispatch_boards()` drops it while `list_boards()` still shows it;
* the archived-slug resurrection guard (`board_is_archived_stub`) and the sanctioned
  re-create;
* the flag defaults on, round-trips both ways, is not materialised by an unrelated write,
  and the `set-dispatch` verb admits and excludes.

`scripts/run_tests.sh tests/hermes_cli/test_kanban_estate_board_dispatch.py` → 9 passed,
0 failed.

prs.title: fix(cli): a resumed session's model follows the profile config, not a stale cached pin
prs.body:
`sessions.model` is written at session creation from whatever `model.default` said at that instant, so it is a CACHE of the config default rather than a record of user intent. `_restore_session_model` (`hermes_cli/cli_model_switch_mixin.py`) restored that cached value unconditionally on every resume, so a settled change to a profile's `model.default` never reached sessions that had already cached the old value — with no warning and no repair. This PR makes the reconciliation the invariant and gives it the config knob to control it.

## Mechanism (current `main`)

- `hermes_cli/cli_model_switch_mixin.py::_restore_session_model` — on resume it calls `stored_session_route(...)` and assigns `self.model = stored_model` from the row whenever the row has a model and the CLI got no `-m`. Nothing there distinguishes a model a user picked from the config default of the day.
- The row's model is written at creation from the then-current `model.default`, and nothing re-derives it when config changes.
- Net effect: change a profile's `model.default` and every session that had already cached the old default keeps running the old model on resume.

## Change

A stored model is now honoured only when the row records a deliberate pick — and the reconciliation is operator-configurable.

1. **`session.model_policy`** (new knob; root or per-lane `config.yaml`, inheriting exactly like `model.default` because it is read from the same resolved config `load_cli_config()` produces):

   ```yaml
   session:
     model_policy: follow_config   # default
   ```

   - `follow_config` *(default)* — a stored model is a cache: honoured only for a row that records a deliberate pick (the route stamp below) **and** that came from an interactive source; everything else reconciles to the resolved config default.
   - `never_pin` — no stored model is ever restored; config always wins.

   An unknown value is a **config error**, never a silent fallback: `resolve_session_model_policy()` raises `SessionModelPolicyError`, and `validate_config_structure()` reports it as an `error` `ConfigIssue` (so `hermes doctor` and the startup check name it instead of a session that simply will not open). Only an absent/`null` value means "unset".

2. **The repair no longer restamps the route it just rejected.** A `provider` key beside the model IS pick-provenance, so writing the config's provider back onto the reconciled row turned it into a permanent "a user chose this" and handed the pin straight back at the next config change. The repaired row now records the model that actually ran and **deletes** the stale route keys (top-level and nested `gateway_runtime`), so it stays a cache and reconciles again next time.

3. **Non-interactive sources never pin** — `kanban`, `cron`, `oneshot`, `bot_peer_dm`, `peer`, `webhook`, `delegation`, `subagent`, `background_review`: no user was present to choose, so a stray route key cannot resurrect a stale pin. A resumed **one-shot** (`hermes_cli/oneshot.py::_apply_stored_session_runtime`) treats the stored route as a cache too, so `hermes -q --resume` cannot restore a pin either. A source this change does not know falls back to the conservative route check (honour the stored model), so an unknown surface is never silently clobbered.

4. **Pick-provenance is unchanged** (and already written by every deliberate switch): a `provider` at the top level of `model_config` or under its nested `gateway_runtime`, written by the CLI's `_persist_model_switch_to_session`, the messaging gateway's `SessionDB.update_session_model(provider=...)`, and the TUI/desktop's `_runtime_model_config`. That stamp is the only thing that authorises a stored model ≠ the config default.

5. **The RETENTION pin is not touched.** `sessions.pinned` (col 47, `set_session_pinned`, `hermes_state_sessions.py:992`) is a *different* thing that shares the name: `sessions.model` / `model_config` is ROUTING, `sessions.pinned` is RETENTION. Nothing here reads or writes it, so prune/archive exemption keeps working — "do not pin models implicitly" must not break it.

When the profile config names no default there is nothing to reconcile against, so the ordinary stored-route restore runs unchanged, preserving its credential re-resolution and its in-place `agent.switch_model` swap — except under `never_pin`, where a stored model is never restored at all.

## Relation to existing reports

This is the CLI resume seam. It shares the symptom with #101514 (a profile session is pinned to its stored model on resume) but fixes a **different root cause**: #101514 describes the gateway seam (`tui_gateway/server.py` `_stored_session_runtime_overrides` / `_sync_agent_model_with_config`), whereas this change is `hermes_cli/cli_model_switch_mixin.py::_restore_session_model`. The two are complementary. #89084 asks for the same "follow config on resume" property as a config option; this delivers it — plus the config option (`session.model_policy`) that asks for.

I searched for existing PRs to make sure this isn't a duplicate (`gh search prs --repo NousResearch/hermes-agent "session model resume"`) and found none matching this file or seam.

## Verification

Red→green at the PR head (`2996c2bd69c9d2d28bf8d7a9ce7038a64e633cdb`; its code commit is `e141e5110c7fd6376211375a9966726b01bb4b70` — the tip adds one docs-only commit) with the repo's own runner:

- `tests/hermes_cli/test_session_model_follows_config.py` → **28 passed**. New cases: a stale cached pin is reconciled **and repaired in the store** so it cannot return (including on a *second* config change), a stamped deliberate pick survives, every non-interactive source is a cache even with a route key, `never_pin` ignores every stored model, and an unknown knob value is refused.
- Red-first, both ways: (a) with the base tree the file is a collection error, and (b) with only the pre-fix repair restored (route restamped instead of deleted) the two "the pin cannot return" tests fail — so they exercise real behaviour, not a mirror.
- `tests/hermes_cli/test_resume_model_restore.py`, `test_oneshot_resume.py`, `test_model_persist_one_shape.py`, `test_model_switch_reasoning_flag.py`, `tests/tui_gateway/test_custom_provider_session_persistence.py` → unchanged failure sets against the same files on the base tree (the 8 failures are pre-existing in this sandbox, identical in both arms).
- Regression sweep, per-file isolated (each file its own process and `HERMES_HOME`, the runner's isolation model) over 146 files of the CLI/config surface — `tests/hermes_cli/test_config*.py`, `test_cli_init.py`, `test_oneshot*.py`, `test_resume*.py`, `test_model*.py`, `test_session*.py`: **identical failure sets on both arms** (214 ids at the head, 215 at the base). The only delta is a single id that fails in *both* arms and is merely labelled `ERROR` on one and `FAILED` on the other (`test_session_owner_backfill.py`, which trips the harness's real-home file-I/O guard in either tree).
- Live before/after against the live tree's own `_restore_session_model` (live install venv, real `SessionDB` row, config default `deepseek-flash`, stored `deepseek-v4-pro`): **before** → `deepseek-v4-pro` restored and the row left as-is; **after** → `deepseek-flash`, the row repaired to `deepseek-flash` with the stale route deleted, and the override warned on stderr. Under `never_pin` the same deliberate-pick row is ignored; an unknown policy value raises `SessionModelPolicyError`.

Authored with AI assistance (Hermes Agent); diff verified manually.

prs.title: fix(cron): a profile with no model of its own inherits the host default
prs.body:
## What

A cron job created in a **named profile** whose `config.yaml` carries no `model:` block dies before
it can spawn. Two arms, one symptom:

**Arm 1 — the scheduler raises instead of falling back.** `_load_cron_job_config`
(`cron/scheduler.py`) resolves the run's model from the *active profile's* config only
(`load_user_config_effective` reads that one file — profiles are self-contained), then raises
`RuntimeError: … has no model configured (job.model=None, HERMES_MODEL='', config.yaml model.default
missing or empty)`.

**Arm 2 — `pinned=True` silently pins nothing.** `create_job` locks `_main_model_pin()`'s
`(None, None)` onto the job when the profile has no resolvable main model, so it returns `success`
while persisting a **dead, unpinned** job. Same silent-failure class.

## Fix

- `cron/jobs.py`
  - `host_default_model(active_home)` reads the **HOST root** config's `model.default` + provider
    (`get_default_hermes_root()`), consulted only when the active home names no model of its own.
  - `_main_model_pin()` inherits it, and passes the host provider as `requested` to
    `resolve_runtime_provider` (without it the provider resolve raises `AuthError` in a profile with
    no `model.provider`).
  - `create_job` and `_apply_pin_update` **refuse** (`ValueError`, naming the profile whose store it
    is) when a pin resolves no model at all, instead of persisting an inert job.
- `cron/scheduler.py` — `_load_cron_job_config` falls back to the host default (model **and**
  provider) so an unpinned one-shot runs; the raise now names the profile's store and fires only
  when **no** model resolves anywhere.
- `tools/cronjob_tools.py` — surface the pin refusal as a tool error.

## Why host fallback

The host root config is where the operator's default lives; a named profile with no `model:` of its
own has no default to run unpinned jobs on. Reading the host root is the same layer the root
profile's own jobs use, so an unpinned job in a profile behaves like an unpinned job in the root.
A profile that *does* set `model:` is untouched (a regression test pins that).

## Tests

`tests/cron/test_cron_model_host_fallback.py` — 7 regression tests (scheduler inherits host model;
profile model still wins; raise names the profile and only fires when nothing resolves; pin inherits
host model+provider; pin refuses instead of persisting a dead job; pinned create locks the host
model).

- new suite: **7 passed**
- `tests/cron/test_cron_pinned_job_fallback.py` + `tests/cron/test_cron_provider_pin.py`:
  **25 passed** (no regression)

prs.title: fix(gateway): a platform verdict may not survive a gateway life boundary
prs.body:
## What is broken

`gateway_state.json` can report `platforms.<name>.state == "connected"` for a platform that no
longer exists, because a platform verdict survives a **gateway life boundary** and no reader
validated its writer identity.

* Write side: `gateway/status.py::_prepare_runtime_status_update` keeps every platform key without
  a `:` when `clear_profile_platforms=True` — i.e. the default profile's OWN adapters, `api_server`
  included — while the same write restamps `pid`/`start_time`/`updated_at` for the new process. The
  first write of a new life (`gateway/run_startup.py`, `gateway_state="starting"`,
  `clear_profile_platforms=True`, `reload_existing=True`) therefore left the file with a live pid, a
  fresh `updated_at`, and `api_server: connected` from the **previous, dead** life.
* Read side: the ownership predicate existed and was tested
  (`hermes_cli/web_server_gateway.py::_owned_profile_platforms`) but was applied only to the
  cross-profile aggregation map. `hermes_cli/web_routers/status.py::_project_gateway_platforms`
  read the RAW map while its docstring claimed an upstream writer-identity filter that did not run
  on that path. `_component_health` counts `state in {"connected","running","ok"}`, so the dead
  platform was certified healthy.

## Change

**B1 (write side, root cause).** `_prepare_runtime_status_update` now applies a life-boundary rule at
the one chokepoint every writer passes: when the record being merged into names a different
`(pid, start_time)`, every inherited platform entry that cannot name the current life is re-stamped
`state="starting"` (never a healthy state) with its old verdict parked under `stale_*`. Colon-keyed
and flat keys are treated identically; entries with no writer stamps fail closed.
`clear_profile_platforms` keeps its current meaning and the stopped-gateway behaviour is untouched.

**B2 (read side, defence in depth).** The ownership predicate is lifted into a single home,
`gateway/status.py::runtime_platforms_owned_by`, and `own_profile_platforms_owned_by` applies it to
a runtime record's own map. It is now used by the `components.platforms` verdict (`/api/status`), the
`/api/messaging/platforms` channels payload, and `tools/send_message_tool.py` (which already checked
the record's pid liveness but must also refuse a foreign-life entry).
`_owned_profile_platforms` (cross-profile) delegates to the shared predicate. The new `stale_*` keys
join `_PRIVATE_PLATFORM_ENTRY_KEYS` so process recon never projects onto the public endpoint.

`updated_at` semantics and the absence of a heartbeat field are unchanged.

## Tests

* Writer negative control (`tests/gateway/test_status.py`): seeds a record from life L1, runs the
  boot write for life L2, asserts `api_server` is no longer `connected`. On the pre-fix tree this
  fails with `assert 'connected' == 'starting'` — the RED.
* Colon-keyed/flat key-agnostic downgrade; current-life entry untouched (no regression).
* `tests/hermes_cli/test_web_server_gateway_topology.py`: a live-pid record carrying a foreign-life
  `api_server` entry is not counted healthy by `/api/status` and not reported connected by the
  messaging payload; `stale_*` never projects.
* `tests/tools/test_send_message_tool.py`: a foreign-life entry no longer vouches for the gateway's
  credentials.
* `tests/hermes_cli/test_web_server_messaging_stale_runtime.py` stays green.

## Blast radius / rollback

Touches the status write/read path plus one tool. Rollback = revert these files. Affects the desktop
dashboard platform panel and the cross-profile aggregation, both of which now see only verdicts the
live process wrote.

prs.title: fix(bootstrap): only an entry point finishes a source update or re-execs
prs.body:
## What

`hermes_bootstrap` is imported by every entry-point module, so its module body also runs for a plain `import`. Two things in that body are only correct for a process that is *becoming* the CLI:

- finishing an armed source update (`prepare_launch`), and
- `os.execv`-ing the relaunched interpreter.

Measured 2026-10-01: a unit-test module imported the live CLI; the bootstrap completed a real source update against the live checkout and then `os.execv`-ed the pytest session away. Instrumentation saw three such routes from one test module (2026-10-04).

## Change

Both blocks are now gated on `_launched_as_entry_point()`, which reads the **importer's** frame. (`__name__` of `hermes_bootstrap` itself is `hermes_bootstrap` either way, so it cannot be used.)

A launch is one of:

- the module that imports us **is** the program — `python main.py`, `python -m hermes_cli.main`, `runpy` with `run_name="__main__"`; or
- the module that imports us was **itself imported directly by the program** — a console-script wrapper's `from hermes_cli.main import main`, and `python -c "import <launcher>"`.

The second clause is required by the product: `relaunch_command` reconstructs a relaunch for `argv[0] == "-c"` (`hermes_cli/venv_sync.py`), so that launch mode is first-class and must keep the tail.

Anything deeper is a library caller inside a longer-running process (a test module under pytest) and is withheld.

The withheld path is not silent: when armed completion state is present it prints exactly one line naming the command that finishes the update, suppressed under pytest. `recover_if_needed`, `activate_dependencies`, the Happy Eyeballs socket shim and the scratch TMPDIR keep running for **every** importer.

## Tests

New `tests/test_bootstrap_launch_tail_guard.py` — a fake tree with stub modules and a recording `venv_sync`, run in child processes with `-S` so the fake tree's modules win over the interpreter's editable finder:

- a module *inside another program* imports the CLI → the tail does **not** run (the incident route);
- `-m hermes_cli.main`, `-c "import hermes_cli.main"` (the launcher mode above) and a script keep the tail;
- with a relaunch armed, an import neither re-execs nor warns;
- armed completion state is announced once on the withheld path, and suppressed under pytest;
- **negative control:** with the guard forced open, the incident route *does* run the tail — the assertions bite.

Red before this change (4 failed / 3 passed on the pre-change bytes); green after (7 passed) on the checkout's own test environment (CPython 3.14.7, pytest 9.1.1).

- `tests/test_bootstrap_launch_tail_guard.py`: **7 passed**
- `tests/test_hermes_bootstrap.py`: **27 passed, 12 skipped** (identical to the pre-change baseline)
- `tests/pm/test_source_update_launch.py`: **16 passed** (the 5 tests that drive the real bootstrap — `test_real_bootstrap_reexecs_before_app_imports[script|module|command]`, `test_failed_launch_completion_degrades_to_a_warning[argv0|argv1]` — were 5 passed before the change as well)

## Scope / rollback

One file (`hermes_bootstrap.py`) plus one new test module. Rollback is a revert of this commit.

prs.title: feat(cli): add `hermes wall` — broadcast one message to every registered agent
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Adds `hermes wall "<message>"` — send ONE message to EVERY registered agent, and make the process exit status answer the only question an operator asks before taking a shared service down: **did the whole fleet actually receive this?**

This is the residual layer of the fleet's "critical section" construct: an operator taking a shared service down broadcasts a warning to every served agent and needs to know the broadcast landed. `hermes wall` is that broadcast.

Design:

- **Roster** from the gateway's own registry chokepoint, `hermes_cli.profiles.profiles_to_serve(multiplex=True)` — never a hard-coded list. A registered profile the gateway does not serve is reported `unroutable`, not silently skipped.
- **Delivery** reuses the existing peer transport (`hermes peer dm --json`), so idempotency-key derivation, replay and admission stay in one place instead of growing a second delivery path.
- **Verify the settle.** A target counts as reached only on `result=delivered`, or on a terminal `delivered` row in the delivery ledger for a receipt that settled. An unanswered receipt is retried once and then reported NOT reached — a send is not an answer.
- **Never truncate.** A body already carrying a truncation marker is refused outright; a body over `wall.chunk_max_chars` is split at sentence/clause boundaries into ordinal-labelled parts, and every non-final part carries an explicit `[continues in N/M]` marker. The parts arrive as separate messages in separate turns, so a mid-clause ending is otherwise indistinguishable from a transport clip.
- **Exit status:** 0 only when every registered agent is confirmed reached; 1 when any is not; 2 when the broadcast is refused before anything is sent.

## Related Issue

Fixes #

## Type of Change

- [x] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality)

## Changes Made

- `hermes_cli/subcommands/wall.py` — the `hermes wall` verb (`build_wall_parser`, `cmd_wall`, `run_wall`, the split/settle logic).
- `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py` — the `wall` config section (`chunk_max_chars`, `max_chunks`, `max_workers`, `retry_delay_seconds`, `peer_timeout_seconds`).
- `hermes_cli/main.py` — register `build_wall_parser` next to the peer parser.
- `tests/hermes_cli/test_wall.py` — 23 cases pinning the roster, the settle rule, the retry-then-not-reached rule, the clause-aligned split with its continuation marker, and both refusal paths.

## How to Test

1. `pytest tests/hermes_cli/test_wall.py -q` → 23 passed.
2. `hermes wall --help` renders the verb.
3. Against a live gateway: `hermes wall "switching model pins, expect a slow turn" --reason deploy` — exits 0 only when every served agent's delivery settles.

## Stack note (read before merging)

`hermes wall` is a **consumer of the peer-delivery stack**. It needs:

- `hermes peer dm --wait <s>` and the delivery result envelope (`--json` `result` / `delivery_id`), and
- `tools.bot_delivery_queue.read_record`, its settle cross-check (guarded import; degrades to transport-result-only if absent).

Accordingly this branch is that peer-delivery chain (through `feat/bot-delivery-drain-profile-scope`, layer 5) **plus** the wall commit. Once the chain's PRs land on `main`, this PR's diff recomputes to the wall commit alone. If it is preferred to keep the chain in its existing PR, the wall commit can instead be applied on top of that branch.

## Checklist

- [x] Tested on macOS

prs.title: feat(sessions): make state.db write patience configurable
prs.body:
## Why

A shared `state.db` is legitimately held for multi-second stretches by sibling Hermes processes (VACUUM after auto-prune, a TRUNCATE checkpoint at close on a large WAL, a long FTS pass). The two write budgets were compiled constants — 20s routine / 60s transcript — so a host whose maintenance window exceeds them could only widen them by editing code. When the transcript append loses that race the whole turn aborts as `session_persistence_failed` even though the store is healthy and merely busy, discarding the turn's already-done model work; failing and retrying re-runs — and re-pays for — the entire turn.

## What

The two budgets become `sessions.*` config keys, canonical in `config.yaml` and mirrored into the env carriers `hermes_state` already reads — the same shape as the existing `cjk_fts` / `search_slow_ms` bridges:

| config key | env carrier | default |
|---|---|---|
| `sessions.transcript_write_patience_s` | `HERMES_TRANSCRIPT_WRITE_PATIENCE_S` | 60 |
| `sessions.write_patience_s` | `HERMES_WRITE_PATIENCE_S` | 20 |

- `SessionDB` resolves them once per handle at construction via `routed_sessions_setting`, so a multiplexed profile reads its own `config.yaml` rather than the launch profile's env slot.
- A value is materialised on the handle only when it actually **differs** from the compiled default, which keeps the class attributes the single visible source of the defaults and leaves the existing monkeypatch seam (`SessionDB._WRITE_PATIENCE_S = ...`) working untouched.
- A non-positive or unparseable value is ignored: patience may be raised, never removed (a zero-wait writer would reinstate the exact abort this knob exists to prevent).
- The observation-only activity budget and the `_COMPRESSION_BUSY_WAIT_S` lease wait stay compiled-in — the latter is a correctness boundary, not a tuning knob.
- Bridged in both entry points: `gateway.run._SESSIONS_ENV_BRIDGE` and `hermes_cli.cli_config_load._mirror_config_to_env`.

**No behaviour change when the keys are unset.**

## Tests

- `tests/hermes_state/test_write_patience_config.py` — resolution and precedence, the budget the write path is actually handed (config → env → handle → `patience_s`), the unconfigured-default negative control, the scope guard on the non-configurable budgets, and a multi-second sibling lock hold ridden out.
- `tests/gateway/test_write_patience_config_bridge.py` — `config.yaml` → env for both the gateway bridge and the CLI mirror.

8 of the 18 new tests fail against the pre-change file (`KeyError: 'HERMES_WRITE_PATIENCE_S'`, wrong budget, missing config keys) and pass with it; the default/scope cases pass at both ends.

Two failures in the surrounding suites were measured on the pristine base too and are unrelated to this change: `tests/hermes_state/test_write_lock_patience.py::test_exhausted_patience_names_the_real_cause` (a 2s hold against a 0.2s budget no longer forces the failure on this base) and `tests/gateway/test_multiplex_residue_parity.py::test_stale_served_turn_never_recreates_archived_profile` when run in the same session as `tests/hermes_state/test_fts_cjk_bigram.py` (cross-file pollution).

issues.title: [BUG] Telegram MarkdownV2 skips escaping link labels and blockquote text, causing plain-text fallback
issues.body:
## Quick Summary

With Telegram MarkdownV2 enabled, reserved characters in link labels and blockquote text can cause Telegram to reject a reply. PicoClaw then falls back to plain text, losing formatting for the entire reply.

The converter treats complete links and blockquote lines as verbatim entities, bypassing the escaping required inside their text.

## Environment & Tools

- **PicoClaw Version:** v0.3.1, commit `2cf030d2fd3b871d7ec17e3be34c24688aac76da`
- **Go Version:** Binary built with Go 1.25.11
- **AI Model & Provider:** `gpt-6.1-sol`, OAuth
- **Operating System:** Debian GNU/Linux 13 (trixie), x86_64
- **Channels:** Telegram, direct chat
- **Configuration:** `channel_list.telegram.settings.use_markdown_v2: true`

## 📸 Steps to Reproduce

1. Enable Telegram MarkdownV2.
2. Have the bot deliver a reply containing either of these examples:

   **Link label containing a period:**
   ```markdown
   Please refer to the PicoClaw website. ([picoclaw.io](https://picoclaw.io/))
   ```

   **Blockquote containing parentheses around a link:**
   ```markdown
   > **Please refer to the source code.** ([github.com](https://github.com/sipeed/picoclaw))
   ```

## ❌ Actual Behavior

Existing conversations produced Telegram HTTP 400 errors for unescaped periods and opening parentheses:

```text
Bad Request: can't parse entities: Character '.' is reserved and must be escaped with the preceding '\'
```

```text
Bad Request: can't parse entities: Character '(' is reserved and must be escaped with the preceding '\'
```

PicoClaw then logs:

```text
MarkdownV2 parse failed, falling back to plain text
```

The reply is delivered as plain text, losing formatting.

## ✅ Expected Behavior

Escape reserved characters in link display text and blockquote text while preserving the intended formatting.

The examples above should be converted to:

```markdown
Please refer to the PicoClaw website\. \([picoclaw\.io](https://picoclaw.io/)\)
```

```markdown
> *Please refer to the source code\.* \([github\.com](https://github.com/sipeed/picoclaw)\)
```

Link destinations should follow their own MarkdownV2 escaping rules.

## 💬 Additional Context

Relevant source:

https://github.com/sipeed/picoclaw/blob/2cf030d2fd3b871d7ec17e3be34c24688aac76da/pkg/channels/telegram/parse_markdown_to_md_v2.go#L70

- `verbatimEntities` includes `[`, `>`, and `**>`.
- `processText` writes these matched spans unchanged, skipping escaping inside link labels and blockquote text.
- Existing tests do not cover unescaped punctuation in these contexts.

The converter and its test file are byte-identical between v0.3.1 and the inspected main commit `bbf6893ca7afad27f1d00a0f5a45982a549c6ed6`.

Telegram MarkdownV2 reference:

https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#markdownv2-style

issues.title: 智能路由：turn 中途不重判、无重复调用熔断，轻量模型可空转烧掉千万 token
issues.body:
## 现象

智能路由（`agents.defaults.routing`）把一轮简单对话交给轻量模型后，该轻量模型在**单轮内空转 222 次 LLM 调用**，约 9 分钟内累计消耗约 **1310 万输入 token**（约 13,098,285 tokens），输出内容几乎恒定、无任何有效进展。整轮最终被手动中止。

## 复现数据（真实事故 trace）

| 指标 | 值 |
| --- | --- |
| 时间窗口 | 09:00:27 – 09:09:48（约 561 秒） |
| LLM 调用次数 | 222 次（`iterations_total=222`） |
| 命中模型 | 100% 为轻量模型（一次都未切回主力） |
| prompt tokens | 从 11,218 逐步涨到 78,679 |
| 累计输入 tokens | ≈ 13,098,285 |
| 每次输出 tokens | 恒定 75 / 76（退化循环） |
| turn.end 状态 | `aborted`，`duration_ms=563919` |

特征：每一轮响应都带着几乎相同的工具调用（同名工具、近似参数），模型在"调用工具 → 得到结果 → 再调用同一个工具"之间循环，上下文随工具结果不断膨胀（prompt tokens 持续上涨），但没有任何收敛迹象。

## 原因分析（四个叠加因素）

1. **turn 中途不重判模型**
   路由只在 turn 开始时判定一次并选定模型档位，之后整轮固定不变。即使上下文已经从 1 万 token 涨到 7 万+、工作明显是工具密集型，也不会升级回主力模型。

2. **没有重复调用熔断**
   对"连续多轮返回完全相同的工具调用"没有任何检测。模型退化循环时只受 `max_tool_iterations` 约束，默认 50 轮仍会消耗大量 token；本例中循环甚至在校验之外持续了 222 轮。

3. **插话消息可绕过硬性迭代上限**
   迭代循环的继续条件类似：

   ```go
   for iteration < max_tool_iterations || len(pendingMessages) > 0 || graceful
   ```

   pending（steering）消息存在时循环不受 `max_tool_iterations` 限制，等于没有硬上限，一个坏循环可以无限延长。

4. **轻量模型池整体失败时直接报错**
   轻量模型的候选全部失败（服务不可用、密钥失效）时，本轮直接以错误结束，而不是退回主力模型。

## 建议

- **轮内升级（escalation）**：轻量模型单次响应 prompt tokens 超阈值（如 32k）或连续 N 轮（如 3）调用工具时，本轮剩余请求切换到主力模型；每轮最多升级一次。
- **重复调用熔断（repeat breaker）**：连续 N 次（如 5）出现"同名工具 + 相同参数（规范化后）"即中止本轮，并返回明确提示；对所有模型档位生效。
- **steering 硬顶**：插话延长轮次需有绝对上限（例如 `max_tool_iterations × 3`，且不低于 `max_tool_iterations + 20`）。
- **轻量池失败回退**：轻量模型候选全部失败时自动改走主力池，而不是直接失败。

上述四项守卫已在 fork 中实现并附集成测试（重复熔断、prompt 升级、工具强度升级、轻量池失败回退），可作为参考：

- 实现提交：`cnbillsomeday/picoclaw@24382d7c`
- 发布：https://github.com/cnbillsomeday/picoclaw/releases/tag/session-header-v1.3.1

## 📝 Description

Adds a native Sendblue channel so users can text a PicoClaw agent over iMessage/SMS and get its answer on the same phone. The guide covers fresh free-account setup, human phone/contact verification, model prerequisites, secrets, and receive-webhook registration.

This draft proposes a self-contained channel through the existing factory and shared webhook server. It validates the secret, receiving line and sender; normalizes direct-message context; deduplicates the last 4096 accepted handles in memory; and uses the existing outbound workers. Configuration supports named instances, redacted secrets, environment overrides, persistence, and credential-triggered reloads.

Scope is direct-message text. Groups/status callbacks are ignored; incoming attachments produce an explicit unsupported-attachment notice. There is no durable inbox or exactly-once guarantee. Ambiguous sends are not automatically retried, because the provider endpoint has no idempotency key.

issues.title: [capability] add-pi: pick the group's own provider, not the install's whole gateway list
issues.body:
Follow-up from #4129 (`/add-pi`).

## The problem

`PI_GATEWAY_PROVIDERS` is an install-wide env var, but a provider is a **per-group** property (`container_configs.provider`). The container uses that list to decide which providers get a gateway placeholder in `auth.json` and which one becomes pi's `defaultProvider`.

When the gateway holds keys for more than one provider — say DeepSeek for one group and OpenAI for another — `resolveDefaultProvider` gets a set with two members, refuses to guess, writes no default, and pi falls back to its own built-in first choice: Anthropic. That is usually the one provider the gateway has no key for, so the group fails auth for a reason that has nothing to do with how it was configured.

The container-config env is per-group, so this could be resolved per group, but the payload currently has no per-group channel to carry it.

## What should be possible

A group switched to pi answers on the model its operator chose for **that group**, whether or not the same gateway holds keys for other providers. Multi-provider installs should not silently land on Anthropic.

## Options

1. **Per-group provider list.** Carry the selected provider in the group's container config (or `settings.json`) instead of a shared env var, so the payload reads one group's answer rather than the install's superset.
2. **Fail loudly.** If the declared set is ambiguous and nothing named a default, refuse with a diagnostic naming the possible providers, instead of letting pi pick Anthropic.

Option 2 is cheaper and strictly better than today; option 1 is the real fix.

## Notes

- The single-provider case (what #4129 was tested with) works today; this only bites multi-provider installs.
- `PI_DEFAULT_PROVIDER` exists as a manual override, which is what makes today's behaviour survivable rather than broken.

issues.title: [capability] add-pi: decide mid-turn text delivery instead of silently keeping result-only
issues.body:
Follow-up from #4129 (`/add-pi`).

## The problem

pi's payload declares `textDelivery: 'result'`, so only the last assistant text of a turn reaches the chat. A turn shaped like "message A → tool call → message B" delivers B and silently drops A.

The Claude provider declares `mid-turn-complete` precisely to avoid this: the poll loop scans mid-turn `text` segments for completed message blocks and delivers them as they are emitted. The pi payload emits `activity` for every SDK event but does not surface assistant text segments as `text` events, so nothing mid-turn can ever be delivered.

This is a decision I made while porting, not something pi forces — but it is currently undocumented, which makes it look like an oversight. Two outcomes are acceptable; silence is not.

## What should be possible

Either:

1. **Deliver mid-turn text.** pi emits `message_end` per completed assistant message, which is enough to surface each finished text block as a `text` event and declare `mid-turn-complete`. Needs checking against pi's compaction continuation, where assistant messages also appear — a mid-compaction summary must not be delivered as chat.

2. **Keep `result`, with the tradeoff written down.** If mid-turn delivery is genuinely undesirable here (e.g. it interacts badly with the memory/instructions block being wrapped into the opening prompt), record why in `ARCHITECTURE.md` so the next reader does not rediscover it.

## Notes

- Whatever the answer, it should come with a test: the current suites cover turn completion but not "A → tool → B delivers both".
- Related: the payload wraps `systemContext.instructions` into the opening prompt as a `<system>` block. Any mid-turn delivery work should confirm the model never echoes that block back as chat text.

issues.title: [capability] add-pi: rotate a pi continuation that has grown too large to resume
issues.body:
Follow-up from #4129 (`/add-pi`).

## The problem

`AgentProvider` documents `maybeRotateContinuation(continuation, cwd)` as the guard for one specific failure mode:

> a long-lived hub session accumulates days of history — including base64 image blocks the agent Read — and the SDK reloads the whole `.jsonl` on every resume. Past a threshold the first turn alone can exceed the host's idle ceiling, so the container is killed before it ever replies.

pi never shrinks its session file. `compaction` appends entries in place; the JSONL keeps growing. The continuation token is that file's absolute path, so a hub group running for weeks resumes the whole thing on every cold start, and the first turn's cost grows without bound — exactly the shape the interface was added for. The Claude provider answers it; the pi payload currently does not.

## What should be possible

A pi group that has been alive for weeks still answers its first message after a container restart, because the payload decided the continuation was too large or too old and started a fresh session instead — archiving a summary first, the way `ClaudeProvider` does.

## Notes

- `maybeRotateContinuation` is optional on `AgentProvider`; returning a non-null reason is what tells the poll loop to drop the continuation.
- The threshold is provider knowledge: pi's JSONL size is not comparable to Claude's, and the right numbers depend on the model's context window. Worth deciding with whoever runs pi in production — see @chiptoe-svg's note in #4129 about running it on multi-user installs since May.
- The pi payload already has a one-shot *empty*-resume fallback (`isEmptyPiResume`); this is a sibling concern, at the opposite end (too much history rather than none).

issues.title: [bug] ncl groups config add-mount cannot create read-write mounts.

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something is not working as expected

labels.name: triage/unresolved
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer triage. Applied by issue forms

issues.body:
### Affected NanoClaw version or commit

v2026.10.0

### Host platform

macOS

### What happened?

In v2026.10.0, the handler (src/cli/resources/groups.ts) writes readonly: true when --ro is passed and omits the field otherwise. Mount security (src/modules/mount-security/index.ts:368) grants read-write only when mount.readonly === false, so CLI-created mounts are always read-only even when the allowlist root has allowReadWrite: true. docs/SECURITY.md:115 describes the intended behaviour.
Suggested fix: write readonly: false when --ro is absent, or add an explicit --rw flag.

### What did you expect?

Running ncl groups config add-mount without --ro, for a host path whose allowlist root has allowReadWrite: true, should produce a read-write mount inside the group’s containers.

That’s the behaviour docs/SECURITY.md:115 describes: read-write is granted when the mount requests it (readonly: false) and the matched root has allowReadWrite: true. The command’s help also implies it: --ro is presented as the opt-in for read-only, so leaving it out should mean read-write.

Instead the mount is always read-only.
- The handler in src/cli/resources/groups.ts (config add-mount) writes readonly: true when --ro or --readonly is passed. Otherwise it omits the field entirely.
- Mount security, at src/modules/mount-security/index.ts:368, grants read-write only when mount.readonly === false.
- An omitted field therefore always resolves to read-only.

The CLI has no way to create a read-write mount: --ro false is still truthy, and there’s no --rw flag.

### How can we reproduce it?

Environment: NanoClaw v2026.10.0 (release tag), macOS 27.0.1, Docker Desktop, OneCLI 1.42.0, a fresh install via bash nanoclaw.sh.

Create a host directory, for example /Users/<user>/testmount.
Allow it read-write:

> pnpm exec tsx setup/index.ts --step mounts --force -- --json '{"allowedRoots":[{"path":"/Users/<user>/testmount","allowReadWrite":true,"description":"test"}],"blockedPatterns":[]}'

Confirm that ~/.config/nanoclaw/mount-allowlist.json shows "allowReadWrite": true.
3. Add the mount without --ro:

> ncl groups config add-mount --id <ag-id> --host /Users/<user>/testmount --container testmount

Inspect the stored config:

> ncl groups config get --id <ag-id> | grep -A5 additional_mounts

Observed: the entry contains hostPath and containerPath only, with no readonly key.
5. Run ncl groups restart --id <ag-id>.
6. Ask the agent to create a file under /workspace/extra/testmount/.

Observed: the write fails, and the agent reports that the mount is read-only. Nothing is logged as mount REJECTED: the mount is accepted, then silently forced read-only.

Suggested fix: in the config add-mount handler, write readonly: false when --ro/--readonly is absent. Alternatively, add an explicit --rw flag and document that the default is read-only. Either way, the CLI and SECURITY.md would then agree.

Workaround used: setting readonly: false on the existing mount entry through the /manage-mounts skill, then restarting the group.
